# Leandro Gabriel, technical writing portfolio: full text

Source: https://l-g99921.github.io/tw-portfolio/llms.txt


---

URL: https://l-g99921.github.io/tw-portfolio/docs/methodology

# Documentation methodology

The pages on this site follow two public frameworks. Each one answers a different question:

| Framework | Question it answers |
|---|---|
| [Google developer documentation style guide](https://developers.google.com/style) | How should this sentence read? |
| [Diátaxis](https://diataxis.fr/) | What kind of page is this, and where does it go? |

A style guide alone gives you good sentences on pages that are hard to find. A taxonomy alone gives you a clean structure with pages that are tiring to read. I use both.

## Google developer documentation style guide

### What it is

The [Google developer documentation style guide](https://developers.google.com/style) is the public style guide that Google's developer documentation teams use. Many API documentation teams outside Google adopt it because it targets a specific reader: someone who might not be a native English speaker, might be using a screen reader, and is probably scanning for a code sample.

### The rules I lean on most

- **Second person, active voice, present tense.** "The API returns a token," not "A token will be returned by the API."
- **Sentence case.** For headings, buttons, and UI strings: "Manage your usage," not "Manage Your Usage."
- **No filler.** Words like `just`, `simply`, `easily`, and `please` either add nothing or assume the reader finds the task easy.
- **"Can" for ability, "may" only for permission.**
- **No Latin abbreviations.** "For example" instead of "e.g.," and "that is" instead of "i.e."
- **Realistic examples.** Values that look like real data, never `foo` or `bar`.

### Why I use it

It settles hundreds of small decisions in advance, such as capitalization, voice, commas, and list format, so review time goes to accuracy. In a docs-as-code workflow it also gives reviewers something to cite. A pull request comment can link to a rule instead of turning into a debate about taste.

### Where to see it on this site

- Sentence-case headings across the [integration guide](/docs/integration-guide) and the [hardware install guide](/docs/databridge/databridge-installation-guide-atlas-insight).
- Imperative steps in tutorials and how-to guides: "Tap **Connect**," not "You should tap Connect."
- Realistic payloads in the [API reference](/docs/api/powerbox-api), with field names and values from a believable utility data model.
- A list of [words to avoid](/docs/writing-guideline#72-words-to-avoid) in the site's writing guideline, checked by Vale on every pull request.

## Diátaxis

### What it is

[Diátaxis](https://diataxis.fr/) is a documentation framework by Daniele Procida. It sorts technical documentation into four types, based on two questions: is the reader acting or thinking, and are they learning or working?

```mermaid
quadrantChart
    title Diátaxis content types
    x-axis "Action" --> "Cognition"
    y-axis "Study (acquiring skill)" --> "Work (applying skill)"
    quadrant-1 "Reference"
    quadrant-2 "How-to guides"
    quadrant-3 "Tutorials"
    quadrant-4 "Explanation"
```

| Type | Purpose | The reader is thinking | The page has to |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Tutorial** | Learning by doing | "I'm new. Teach me." | Lead to a result that works, every time |
| **How-to guide** | Reaching a goal | "I know the basics. Show me the steps." | Solve one real problem and skip the basics |
| **Reference** | Looking something up | "I need a fact." | Be accurate and complete, with no story |
| **Explanation** | Understanding | "Help me make sense of this." | Give context, history, and trade-offs |

### One page, one type

The rule that matters most is that each page is one type. When a page mixes a tutorial with a reference, beginners get buried in detail and experienced readers wade through hand-holding. When a how-to drifts into explanation, the reader who wants the steps has to skip paragraphs to find them. Asking "what is this page for?" before writing catches most of these problems.

### Where to see it on this site

| Page | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| [Integration guide](/docs/integration-guide) | Explanation and how-to | A deliberate exception. Integration teams read it start to finish, so the architecture and the steps share one page, in separate sections. |
| [API reference](/docs/api/powerbox-api) | Reference | Generated from OpenAPI. No narrative. |
| [Hardware install guide](/docs/databridge/databridge-installation-guide-atlas-insight) | How-to | Assumes the device is in your hands. |
| [Data dictionary](/docs/data-dictionary) | Reference | Fields and storage locations. |
| [BillSense AI](/docs/billsense-ai/overview) | Explanation and how-to | The overview and the troubleshooting steps are separate pages. |
| [PIX](/docs/pix/about-pix) | All four | One tutorial, one how-to, one reference, and one explanation, each on its own page. |
| [Writing guideline](/docs/writing-guideline) | Reference | Rules to look up while writing. |

If you find a page that mixes types without a reason, I'd treat it as a bug.

## Using both

| Level | Question | Framework |
|---|---|---|
| Word | Which word? | Google |
| Sentence | Active or passive? | Google |
| Page | Tutorial or reference? | Diátaxis |
| Site | Where does this page belong? | Diátaxis |

## Where I've applied this

| Where | What I did |
|---|---|
| **Lean Tech / Crane Worldwide Logistics** (Feb 2026 to present) | Senior technical writer (contract). I own the documentation lifecycle and knowledge governance for Crane Worldwide's operational knowledge base in Doc360, working with business analysts and subject matter experts in three regions. |
| **L'Oréal France** (Nov 2025 to Feb 2026) | Defined the documentation strategy for L'Oréal's data infrastructure: dataflows, database schemas, and the lineage from SQL views to Power BI. Moved a team that relied on SharePoint to docs-as-code, with Markdown, Git, Vale-style linting, and code samples validated in CI. |
| **Sephora LATAM** (through Amaris Consulting, 2024 to 2025) | Led the redesign of the documentation architecture for Sephora's retail platforms in Latin America using TOGAF, with one standard across 5+ countries. Redundant documentation dropped by about 30%, measured with a Confluence content audit. Migrated legacy content to Docusaurus and mentored 3 junior writers in docs-as-code. |
| **Itaú Unibanco** (through Zup Innovation, 2022 to 2024) | Owned the official documentation for the PIX APIs, Brazil's instant-payments system (BRL 17T+ a year, 150M+ users). Wrote 37+ endpoint references, integration guides, release notes, and migration guides in a Bitbucket docs-as-code pipeline. Level 1 support tickets on the PIX integration queue fell about 45% in the six months after launch, and developer satisfaction with the docs rose from 3.8 to 4.6 out of 5 (n=60+, quarterly developer experience survey). |
| **Infomed Benner** (2021 to 2022) | Documentation analyst for healthcare software. Rebuilt the documentation framework, rewrote system manuals in plainer language, and took part in software quality control. |
| **This site** | EnergyGrid applies both frameworks to six kinds of reader: developers, integrators, field technicians, end users, support agents, and people who use AI tools with the docs. PIX covers the full Diátaxis set in a domain I worked in. |

### What the work involves

Moving a team onto these frameworks is mostly practical work:

- **Auditing existing docs against Diátaxis** to find pages that try to do two jobs, and proposing how to split them.
- **Writing an adoption plan for the style guide** that works for writers, engineers, and product managers, who each need a different starting point.
- **Setting up review in docs-as-code**, so that style and page-type problems surface in the pull request, before publication.
- **Coaching engineers** to write references that stay references and tutorials that stay tutorials.

If you're rebuilding a documentation system, [get in touch on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/leandro-gabriel-8aab31167/).

## Further reading

- [Google developer documentation style guide](https://developers.google.com/style)
- [Diátaxis](https://diataxis.fr/), with an essay on each content type
- [Writing guideline](/docs/writing-guideline), this site's applied style guide
- [The Documentation System](https://documentation.divio.com/), Daniele Procida's earlier version of the framework

# Writing guideline

This guide defines the standards for all product, technical, UX, and customer-facing documentation produced for the EnergyGrid platform. It builds on two public frameworks:

- **[Google developer documentation style guide](https://developers.google.com/style):** voice, tone, grammar, and formatting.
- **[Diátaxis](https://diataxis.fr/):** content type, structure, and information architecture.

For why these two, see [Documentation methodology](/docs/methodology).

:::tip Quick rule
If this guide doesn't answer your question, follow the Google developer documentation style guide. If the question is "where should this content live?", follow Diátaxis.
:::

---

## 1. Content types (Diátaxis)

Every page belongs to one of four content types. Pages that mix types are the most common source of confusing documentation.

| Type | Purpose | User question | Example in this site |
|------|---------|---------------|----------------------|
| **Tutorial** | Learning by doing | "Teach me." | [Your first EnergyGrid integration in 30 minutes](/docs/tutorial-first-integration) |
| **How-to guide** | Goal-oriented steps | "Show me how to do X." | [Hardware install guide](/docs/databridge/databridge-installation-guide-atlas-insight) |
| **Reference** | Information lookup | "Tell me what this is." | [API reference](/docs/api/powerbox-api), [data dictionary](/docs/data-dictionary) |
| **Explanation** | Conceptual understanding | "Help me understand." | [About PIX](/docs/pix/about-pix), and the architecture sections of the [integration guide](/docs/integration-guide) |

### Rules

- **One type per page.** If a page is doing two jobs, split it.
- **Tutorials are for beginners.** They lead to a result that works. Links to reference wait until the end.
- **How-to guides assume competence.** They remind the reader of the steps instead of teaching them.
- **Reference is accurate and complete.** No opinions, no story.
- **Explanation gives context.** It can branch, compare, and discuss trade-offs.

For more on each content type, see [Documentation methodology](/docs/methodology#diátaxis).

---

## 2. Voice and tone

Following the Google developer documentation style guide:

- **Conversational, but not overly casual.** Friendly without being cute.
- **Confident, never condescending.** Don't say `obviously`, `simply`, `just`, or `easy`.
- **User-focused.** Use second person ("you") and active voice.

### Tone by audience

| Audience | Tone | Example |
|----------|------|---------|
| Developers (API, integration) | Direct, precise, terminology-heavy | "Authenticate the request with a Bearer token in JWT format." |
| End users (app, hardware) | Friendly, instructional, low-jargon | "Plug in the SmartLink. The light blinks blue when it's ready." |
| Support agents (BillSense AI) | Clear, scannable, action-oriented | "If the bill explanation is missing, check the customer's billing-cycle ID." |
| Disclaimers and legal | Direct, factual, plain language | "Estimates are based on past usage and might vary." |

---

## 3. UX writing for in-product text

Microcopy follows the same principles as long-form documentation: be clear first, then be predictable.

### Patterns

- **Errors:** State what went wrong, then what to do. "Couldn't load your usage. Try again or contact support."
- **Success:** Past tense, specific. "Saved your changes."
- **Empty states:** Explain why and offer a next step. "No data yet. Connect your meter to get started."
- **Loading:** Be specific about what's loading. "Loading your usage history…"

### Buttons and links

- Lead with a verb: **View usage**, **Set budget**, **Reset password**.
- Use sentence case, not title case.
- Make link text descriptive. Avoid "click here," and use "learn more" only with context.
- Two to four words is ideal. If a button label is longer, the action is probably too complex for a button.

### Headings

- **Sentence case for everything.** "Manage your energy use," not "Manage Your Energy Use."
- Use action verbs in tutorials and how-to guides. Use noun phrases in reference and explanation.
- Don't end headings with punctuation (except question marks, sparingly).

---

## 4. Data presentation

### General

- Use visuals to simplify, not to decorate.
- Label every axis, legend, and unit.
- Provide a one-line takeaway above or below every chart.
- Right-align numerical columns in tables.

### Chart types

| Use this | When | Avoid |
|----------|------|-------|
| Line chart | Trends over time, continuous data | More than 4 lines on one axis |
| Bar chart | Comparing discrete categories | Decorative effects, 3D |
| Pie or donut | 2–5 segments, simple proportions | Exact comparisons. Use bars instead. |
| Area chart | Cumulative volume over time | Stacked areas with > 3 categories |
| Table | Precise values, dense reference data | Tables when a chart would tell the story |

---

## 5. Accessibility

- Every meaningful image has alt text. Decorative images have empty alt (`alt=""`).
- Color is never the only signal. Pair color with text, an icon, or a pattern.
- Headings follow a strict hierarchy: H1, then H2, then H3. Don't skip levels.
- Touch targets are at least 44×44 px.
- Language avoids idioms and culture-specific references that don't translate.

---

## 6. Naming conventions

Use official product names exactly as defined. Don't invent variants.

**Correct:**
- DataBridge Hub (not DataBridge or Data Bridge)
- SmartLink Plug (not SmartLink or Smart Link)
- BillSense AI (not BillSense or Bill Sense AI)
- PowerBox API (not `Powerbox` or `Power Box API`)
- EnergyGrid (one word, capital E and G)

When introducing a product, use the full name. Subsequent mentions in the same section can use the short form if it's unambiguous.

---

## 7. Grammar and mechanics

These rules align with the Google Developer Documentation Style Guide.

### 7.1 Voice and tense

- **Active voice.** "The system saves your changes," not "Your changes are saved by the system."
- **Present tense for behavior.** "The endpoint returns a 200 response," not "The endpoint will return…"
- **Imperative mood for instructions.** "Click **Save**," not "You should click Save."

### 7.2 Words to avoid

- **`Please`** in instructions. Write "Click **Save**," not `Please click Save`.
- **`Simply`, `just`, `easily`, `obviously`.** They assume the task is easy for the reader.
- **`May`** for ability. Use **`can`**: "You can configure the budget," not "You may configure the budget."
- **`Will`** for current behavior. Use the present tense: "The API returns…," not "The API will return…"
- **Latin abbreviations.** Write `for example` (not e.g.), `that is` (not i.e.), and `and so on` (not etc.).

### 7.3 Capitalization

- **Sentence case** for all headings, button labels, and UI strings.
- **Lowercase** for URLs, email addresses, and file extensions: `.json`, not `.JSON`, for a file on disk. Capitalize the format name itself: JSON, YAML, XML.
- **Capitalize** product names, acronyms (API, JWT, OAuth), and the first word of sentences.

### 7.4 Acronyms

- Spell out on first use, with the acronym in parentheses: "Customer Information System (CIS)".
- Use the acronym alone for the rest of the page.
- Don't introduce an acronym you only use once.

### 7.5 Contractions

Contractions are encouraged in user-facing content (it's, don't, you're). They make text more conversational and accessible.

### 7.6 Numbers

- Use numerals for 10 and above, and spell out zero through nine. In technical contexts (port numbers, status codes, versions, measurements), always use numerals.
- Add commas to numbers 1,000 and above.
- For large round numbers, use abbreviations: 1k, 150k, 2M (only when space is constrained).

### 7.7 Dates and times

- **Long form:** April 24, 2026.
- **In tables:** 2026-04-24 (ISO 8601).
- **12-hour clock:** 9 am, 10:30 pm (lowercase, no period).
- Include the time zone when relevant: "9 am UTC".

### 7.8 Punctuation

- **Oxford comma:** always.
- **Em dash:** avoid in instructions and reference. A period, colon, or comma is almost always clearer and easier to translate.
- **En dash** (–): for ranges, no spaces. "20–30 users", "Mon–Fri".
- **Hyphen** (-): for compound modifiers. "real-time data", "low-power radio".
- **Exclamation points:** rarely. Never in error messages.

### 7.9 Pronouns

- Use **"they/them"** as the default singular pronoun.
- Use **"you"** to address the reader.
- Use **"we"** for the team's recommendations only when needed; default to imperative.

### 7.10 Lists

- Use a bulleted list when order doesn't matter.
- Use a numbered list when order matters.
- Each item starts with a capital letter.
- End each item with a period if any item is a complete sentence; otherwise no terminal punctuation.
- Keep items grammatically parallel.

### 7.11 Code formatting

- **Inline code** for parameters, properties, file names, and command names: `meterId`, `package.json`, `npm install`.
- **Code blocks** with a language hint for runnable code:
  ```bash
  curl https://api.example.com/v1/users
  ```
- Show realistic, runnable examples. Don't use `foo`, `bar`, or `baz` in user-facing samples.

### 7.12 Currency, percentages, and units

- Use the symbol with the numeral, no space: $20.00, 75%, 72°F.
- Use SI units in technical contexts; add the imperial equivalent in parentheses for user-facing content if relevant.

### 7.13 Phone numbers and URLs

- **Phone:** +1-555-123-4567 (with country code, dashes).
- **URLs:** lowercase, no "www." unless required by the host. Don't underline; the link styling handles that.

---

## 8. Pre-publication checklist

Run through this before publishing any page.

### Content type (Diátaxis)

- [ ] The page is one Diátaxis type: tutorial, how-to, reference, or explanation.
- [ ] If it's drifting between types, it's been split into separate pages.

### Audience and purpose

- [ ] The target audience is identified in the first paragraph.
- [ ] The page solves a real task or answers a real question.
- [ ] Out-of-scope topics are explicitly excluded or linked elsewhere.

### Structure

- [ ] H1 → H2 → H3 hierarchy with no skipped levels.
- [ ] Sections are scannable in under 30 seconds.
- [ ] Related pages and next steps are linked.

### Voice and grammar

- [ ] Active voice, present tense, second person.
- [ ] No `please`, `simply`, `just`, `obviously`, `easily`.
- [ ] `Can` instead of `may`; present tense instead of `will`.
- [ ] Sentence case for all headings and UI strings.
- [ ] Oxford commas, and en dashes only for ranges.

### Technical accuracy

- [ ] Every UI label, parameter, and code sample matches the current product.
- [ ] API examples have been run; status codes and payloads are real.
- [ ] Screenshots are dated within the last release cycle.

### Accessibility

- [ ] All images have descriptive alt text.
- [ ] Color isn't the sole carrier of meaning.
- [ ] Tables have header rows; complex tables have captions.

### Code quality

- [ ] Code blocks have language hints.
- [ ] Examples are realistic, not placeholder.
- [ ] Long examples link to a runnable repo or sandbox if possible.

### Publication

- [ ] Owner and last-updated date are present.
- [ ] All review checks (SME, engineering, UX, legal) are complete.
- [ ] No drafts, TODOs, or placeholder text remain.
- [ ] Release notes are logged if the change is user-visible.

---

## 9. Where to look first

When in doubt:

1. Check this guide.
2. Check the [Google developer documentation style guide](https://developers.google.com/style).
3. Check [Diátaxis](https://diataxis.fr/) for content-type questions.
4. Ask in the docs review channel.

For why the portal uses these two frameworks, see [Documentation methodology](/docs/methodology).

# Architecture decision records

Some choices behind this site aren't obvious from the code: why Docusaurus and not MkDocs, why Google's style guide and not Microsoft's, why the API sandbox runs in the browser. Each one had a real alternative. They're recorded here as architecture decision records (ADRs), one short page per decision, so anyone reading the repository can see why things are the way they are.

The format follows [Michael Nygard's original ADR format](https://cognitect.com/blog/2011/11/15/documenting-architecture-decisions): status, context, decision, and consequences. Each record stays short, because the point is the trade-off.

## Why a portfolio has ADRs

A portfolio is a small product, and it has decisions like any other. Writing them down next to the code shows two things at once: the writing samples, and the reasoning behind the system that publishes them. If you're hiring, these pages show what I'd argue for in a planning meeting. If you maintain the site later, start here before changing direction.

## Index

| ADR | Decision | Status |
|-----|----------|--------|
| [001](/docs/adr/001-docusaurus-over-mkdocs) | Docusaurus 3 instead of MkDocs Material | Accepted |
| [002](/docs/adr/002-google-style-over-microsoft) | Google developer style guide instead of Microsoft's | Accepted |
| [003](/docs/adr/003-diataxis-as-page-taxonomy) | Diátaxis at the page level, one type per page | Accepted |
| [004](/docs/adr/004-vale-fail-on-error) | Vale errors fail the build | Accepted |
| [005](/docs/adr/005-openapi-as-source-of-truth) | OpenAPI specs as the source of the API reference | Accepted |
| [006](/docs/adr/006-api-sandbox-in-the-browser) | An API sandbox that runs in the browser | Accepted |

## Adding an ADR

1. Copy the structure of an existing ADR.
2. Number it next in sequence: `007`, `008`, and so on.
3. Set the status to **Proposed** while it's in review. Change it to **Accepted** when it merges, or to **Rejected** with a one-line reason.
4. If it replaces an older ADR, mark the older one **Superseded by ADR NNN** and link both ways.
5. Add it to the index above and to `sidebars.js`.

ADRs aren't deleted. A superseded or rejected record keeps the reasoning from its time.

# Using these docs with AI

More and more developers meet documentation through an AI assistant instead of a browser. The choices that make a page easy for a person to scan, like one purpose per page, clear headings, and complete metadata, also make it easier for a model to retrieve the right passage. This page explains what this site does for AI tools and how to connect one to it.

## Files for AI tools

- **[`llms.txt`](pathname:///llms.txt)** follows the [llmstxt.org proposal](https://llmstxt.org/). It lists the main pages, grouped by project, each with a one-line description, its Diátaxis type, and an absolute URL.
- **[`llms-full.txt`](pathname:///llms-full.txt)** has the Markdown source of every page in `llms.txt`, plus the description of each API, in one file. A small plugin (`plugins/llms-full.js`) rebuilds it on every deploy, so it always matches the site.
- **The OpenAPI specs**, [`openapi.json`](pathname:///openapi.json), [`usage-api-openapi.json`](pathname:///usage-api-openapi.json), and [`pix-api-openapi.json`](pathname:///pix-api-openapi.json), are the source of the API reference pages.

## Why one Diátaxis type per page helps

Every page on this site is one [Diátaxis](https://diataxis.fr/) type, and the type is in its front matter `tags` (see [ADR 003](/docs/adr/003-diataxis-as-page-taxonomy)). For a retrieval pipeline that means:

- **The page's job is known in advance.** A reference page is for looking things up, and a tutorial has steps with a fixed outcome. The pipeline can read the tag instead of guessing.
- **Questions map to page types.** "How do I…" questions can favor how-to pages, and "What is…" questions can favor reference and explanation.
- **Chunks stay coherent.** A tutorial has no reference tables mixed into its steps, so a chunk taken from it still reads as a tutorial.

## Why the OpenAPI specs help

The API pages are generated from the specs, and nobody edits the generated files by hand (see [ADR 005](/docs/adr/005-openapi-as-source-of-truth)). Each spec carries:

- `info.description`: who the API is for, authentication, base URL, conventions, and versioning.
- `info.contact`: who maintains it.
- `tags[].description`: what each group of operations does.
- `servers[]`: the base URLs.

A pipeline that reads a spec gets the contract and its explanation together, and the reference page can't disagree with it, because the page is built from it.

## Connecting a chatbot

From the simplest option to the most precise:

1. **Give it the overview.** Paste `llms.txt` into the conversation. It's enough for questions like "what's on this site?"
2. **Give it everything.** Paste or attach `llms-full.txt`. The site is small enough to fit in the context window of most current models.
3. **Index it.** Load `llms-full.txt` into a vector store, split at the `URL:` separators, and keep each page's URL and Diátaxis tag as metadata to filter on.

## Documenting an AI product

The [BillSense AI pages](/docs/billsense-ai/overview) document an AI feature for the support agents who explain it to customers, not for the engineers who built it. The content is split by job:

- An [overview](/docs/billsense-ai/overview) of what the feature does and its known limits, such as estimated kWh values that can differ slightly from the bill.
- A [user guide](/docs/billsense-ai) for walking a customer through their bill.
- A [troubleshooting reference](/docs/billsense-ai/troubleshooting) organized by symptom, with an escalation path when nothing works.

## Further reading

- [llmstxt.org](https://llmstxt.org/), the proposal this site follows
- [Diátaxis](https://diataxis.fr/)
- [ADR 003](/docs/adr/003-diataxis-as-page-taxonomy): why every page is one Diátaxis type
- [ADR 005](/docs/adr/005-openapi-as-source-of-truth): why the API pages are generated from the specs

# Your first EnergyGrid integration in 30 minutes

In this tutorial you connect to the [PowerBox API](/docs/api/powerbox-api) sandbox and run the two flows every utility integration needs. By the end you'll have:

- An OAuth access token from the utility identity provider
- A customer synced from the utility's customer information system (CIS), with one premise and one meter
- A DataBridge Hub bound to that meter

You'll use `curl` and `jq` so you can copy each command as is. Any HTTP client works if you prefer another one.

If you'd like to understand how PowerBox fits into the platform before you start, read the [integration guide](/docs/integration-guide) first.

:::tip No terminal handy?
Each call in this tutorial is also on its [API reference page](/docs/api/powerbox-api), where you can send it from the browser. The site simulates the sandbox, so you don't need credentials there.
:::

## Before you begin

- A terminal with `curl` and `jq` installed. To install `jq`, run `brew install jq` on macOS or `sudo apt install jq` on Debian and Ubuntu.
- About 30 minutes.
- An empty folder for the tutorial:

    ```bash
    mkdir energygrid-tutorial && cd energygrid-tutorial
    ```

The sandbox uses synthetic customers and doesn't pair any physical device, so you can't break anything. You can repeat the customer sync as often as you like. Binding is different, and Step 4 explains how to start it over.

## Step 1: Get sandbox credentials

EnergyGrid doesn't issue tokens. The utility's identity provider (IDP) does, and the staging environment includes a synthetic IDP for testing.

1. **Request credentials**

    Email `powerbox-sandbox@energygrid.example` with the subject `Sandbox access`. You get a `client_id` and a `client_secret` within one business hour.

    :::note
    This API is a portfolio sample, so this request flow is illustrative. The OAuth call in Step 2 is the one you'd make against a real utility IDP.
    :::

2. **Save them as environment variables**

    ```bash
    export ENERGY_CLIENT_ID=<your-client-id>
    export ENERGY_CLIENT_SECRET=<your-client-secret>
    export ENERGY_BASE_URL=https://staging.api.energygrid.example/v1
    export ENERGY_IDP_URL=https://idp.staging.energygrid.example
    ```

    `ENERGY_BASE_URL` points to staging. Production is at `https://api.energygrid.example/v1`, and your sandbox client can only read from it.

## Step 2: Get an access token

Back-office flows like customer sync and binding use the OAuth 2.0 **client credentials** grant. Customer sign-in uses a different grant, explained in [Configure authentication](/docs/integration-guide#step-2-configure-authentication-oauth).

Request a token with the two scopes this tutorial needs:

```bash
ENERGY_TOKEN=$(curl -sS -X POST \
  "$ENERGY_IDP_URL/oauth/token" \
  -u "$ENERGY_CLIENT_ID:$ENERGY_CLIENT_SECRET" \
  -d "grant_type=client_credentials&scope=customer.sync hardware.bind" \
  | jq -r .access_token)

echo "Token: ${ENERGY_TOKEN:0:12}…"
```

Expected output:

```text
Token: eyJhbGciOiJ…
```

The token lasts about one hour. If a later step returns `401`, run this step again.

## Step 3: Sync a customer

This call asks PowerBox for a customer's profile from the CIS: the account, the service addresses (premises), and the meters at each one. If it works, EnergyGrid can read your CIS, and the rest of the tutorial depends on that.

1. **Run the sync**

    ```bash
    curl -sS -X POST \
      "$ENERGY_BASE_URL/powerbox/customer" \
      -H "Authorization: Bearer $ENERGY_TOKEN" \
      -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      | tee customer.json | jq '{ clientId, AcctStatus, sites: (.customerSites | length) }'
    ```

    Expected output:

    ```json
    {
      "clientId": "123456789",
      "AcctStatus": "A",
      "sites": 1
    }
    ```

    The full response is now in `customer.json`. `"A"` means the account is active, and the sandbox customer has one premise.

2. **Save the meter and premise IDs**

    A premise can have several meters, such as electric and gas. You need one electric meter:

    ```bash
    export METER_ID=$(jq -r '.customerSites[0].meters[] | select(.meterType=="Electric") | .meterId' customer.json | head -n1)
    export PREMISE_ID=$(jq -r '.customerSites[0].externalSiteId' customer.json)

    echo "Premise: $PREMISE_ID"
    echo "Meter:   $METER_ID"
    ```

    Expected output:

    ```text
    Premise: 5113305555
    Meter:   123456789
    ```

Customer sync is idempotent on `clientId`. Running it again refreshes EnergyGrid's copy of the customer instead of creating a new one.

## Step 4: Bind a DataBridge Hub

Now link a DataBridge Hub to the meter from Step 3. In a real installation, the customer scans the QR code on the device and the utility's wireless mesh radio (the home area network) handles pairing. The sandbox accepts the values below and simulates that handshake.

1. **Send the bind request**

    ```bash
    export HEM_PROFILE_ID=$(jq -r '.clientId' customer.json)

    curl -sS -X POST \
      "$ENERGY_BASE_URL/powerbox/bind" \
      -H "Authorization: Bearer $ENERGY_TOKEN" \
      -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      -d "{
        \"hemProfileId\": \"$HEM_PROFILE_ID\",
        \"macAddress\": \"70:B3:D5:4A:1C:9E\",
        \"installCode\": \"A1B2C3D4E5F6A7B8\",
        \"meterId\": \"$METER_ID\",
        \"actionCode\": 1
      }" -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n"
    ```

    Expected output:

    ```text
    200
    ```

    A `200` means the utility's head-end accepted the request. Pairing itself happens afterward. In production it usually finishes within 15 minutes, and it can take up to 48 hours when the radio signal is weak.

2. **Sync again to check the meter**

    ```bash
    curl -sS -X POST \
      "$ENERGY_BASE_URL/powerbox/customer" \
      -H "Authorization: Bearer $ENERGY_TOKEN" \
      | jq --arg meter "$METER_ID" \
        '.customerSites[].meters[] | select(.meterId == $meter)'
    ```

    Expected output:

    ```json
    {
      "meterId": "123456789",
      "meterType": "Electric",
      "unitOfMeasure": "kWh",
      "isAMI": true,
      "rateCode": "RES1",
      "billingCycleId": 1
    }
    ```

    `isAMI: true` means the meter is on the AMI network, which is what the hub needs to read it.

:::caution Binding is not idempotent
Sending the same bind again returns `400` with `errorCode: METER_ALREADY_BOUND`. To start over, send the request with `"actionCode": 0` to release the meter, then send it again with `1`.
:::

## What you built

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    OAuth["OAuth token<br/>(client credentials)"] --> Sync["POST /powerbox/customer"]
    Sync --> Pick["Save meterId<br/>and premise ID"]
    Pick --> Bind["POST /powerbox/bind<br/>(actionCode: 1)"]
    Bind --> Verify["POST /powerbox/customer<br/>(check the meter)"]
```

Four calls: a token, a customer sync, a bind, and a second sync. A production integration makes the same calls, at higher volume.

## Next steps

- [Integration guide](/docs/integration-guide): mTLS, JWT claims, bulk usage data, billing cycles, rate types, and error codes.
- [PowerBox API reference](/docs/api/powerbox-api): every request and response field and status code.
- [DataBridge Hub installation guide](/docs/databridge/databridge-installation-guide-atlas-insight): the customer's side of the bind you ran.

## Troubleshooting

| Problem | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `401` from `/oauth/token` | Wrong `client_id` or `client_secret` | Export the variables again and check for trailing spaces. |
| `401` from `/powerbox/customer` | The token expired | Repeat [Step 2](#step-2-get-an-access-token). |
| `403` from `/powerbox/customer` | The account is locked or closed (`AcctStatus` is `F`, `L`, or `Z`) | Use another sandbox customer, or ask the CIS team to reactivate the test account. |
| `400` from `/powerbox/bind` with `METER_ALREADY_BOUND` | The meter already has a device | Send `actionCode: 0` to release it, then bind again. |
| `400` from `/powerbox/bind` with `INVALID_INSTALL_CODE` | The install code doesn't match the MAC address | Check the device label, where both are printed together. In the sandbox, use the values from [Step 4](#step-4-bind-a-databridge-hub). |
| `customer.json` is empty after Step 3 | The request failed before returning JSON | Run the `curl` command without `tee` and read the error in the response. |

---

URL: https://l-g99921.github.io/tw-portfolio/docs/integration-guide

# PowerBox and BillSense AI integration guide

This guide is for backend engineers at a utility. It covers what you need to connect your systems to EnergyGrid so that the EnergyGrid app, BillSense AI bill analysis, and the DataBridge Hub work for your customers.

The integration has two layers:

1. **Real-time layer (PowerBox API):** middleware you host that handles customer sign-in and profile sync.
2. **Bulk data layer (SFTP or object storage):** scheduled file transfers with usage data (MDM), billing data, billing cycles, and rate information. BillSense AI depends on this layer.

:::tip Prefer to try it first?
The [30-minute tutorial](/docs/tutorial-first-integration) walks through the real-time layer against the sandbox.
:::

## Step 1: Host the PowerBox middleware

The PowerBox API translates between EnergyGrid and your systems. Host it in your own infrastructure, on premises or in your cloud, and make it reachable from EnergyGrid over HTTPS with TLS 1.2 or later.

Protect it with mutual TLS (mTLS), OAuth token validation, or both. IP allowlisting is a common extra layer.

## Step 2: Configure authentication (OAuth)

EnergyGrid uses the **OAuth authorization code flow** with **OpenID Connect (OIDC)** to link the customer's utility account to their EnergyGrid profile.

:::tip Recommendation
Use OIDC. If your identity provider doesn't support it yet, SAML also works, but most utility partners are moving to OIDC.
:::

### Authentication flow

1. The mobile app sends a token request to the utility identity provider (IDP).
2. The customer signs in on the utility's sign-in page with their existing credentials.
3. The IDP returns an authorization code to the mobile app.
4. The mobile app exchanges the code for a token with the utility IDP.
5. The token response returns to the app.
6. The app sends the token to the EnergyGrid backend.
7. EnergyGrid validates the token against the utility IDP.
8. After validation, EnergyGrid issues its own internal session token for subsequent API calls.

:::note
EnergyGrid uses the utility IDP only for the first sign-in. After it validates the token, EnergyGrid runs the session with its own token. EnergyGrid doesn't store customers' personally identifiable information (PII).
:::

### JWT claims

The claims in the JSON Web Token (JWT) vary by utility. The two common patterns:

| Utility model | Claim used |
|---------|-----------|
| Business partner model | `BPID` (Business Partner ID) |
| Profile-based model | `subject`, custom claims, or Profile ID |

The claim must resolve to a **unique, permanent customer identifier** (see `clientId` in [Step 3](#step-3-customer-synchronization)).

### Login endpoint

**Endpoint:** `POST /powerbox/login`

Authenticates a utility customer against your customer database.

**Request payload:** OAuth token (Bearer header)

**Response (success, HTTP 200):**

```json
{
  "clientId": "123456789"
}
```

**Response (error, HTTP 401 or 404):**

```json
{
  "errorCode": 1
}
```

| Field | Data type | Notes |
|-------|-----------|-------|
| `clientId` | Alphanumeric | Unique customer identifier within the utility |

For every error code, see [Appendix A](#error-codes).

## Step 3: Customer synchronization

After sign-in, EnergyGrid fetches the customer's account details, service addresses (premises), and meter configuration from your customer information system (CIS).

**Endpoint:** `POST /powerbox/customer`

EnergyGrid calls this endpoint right after login, to get current customer data. It calls it again whenever a token expires, the customer signs out, or the customer reinstalls the app.

**Request payload:** OAuth token (Bearer header)

### The data model

| Concept | What it identifies | Examples |
|---------|--------------------|----------|
| **Client ID** | The person (sign-in profile). Stays the same when they move. | Business Partner ID (BPID), Business Partner Number (BPN), Profile ID |
| **Account number** | The billing account. Changes when the customer moves. | Contract account number |
| **External site ID (premise number)** | The physical location. Stays the same between tenants. | Premise number, site number |
| **Meter ID** | The physical meter. Permanent and unique. | Utility meter ID |

**Key relationships:**

- One person (`clientId`) can have multiple premises (`customerSites`).
- One premise can have multiple meters (`meters`).
- Account number plus premise ID identifies one site in EnergyGrid.
- If only one premise or meter exists, `isPrimary` defaults to `true`.

:::note Detecting a tenant move
When premise and meter IDs stay the same between tenants, EnergyGrid detects when a new tenant moves in and removes the premise from the previous tenant's client ID. When two client IDs share the same account number and premise, EnergyGrid treats them as a shared account: several sign-in profiles with access to the same premises.
:::

### Response (full model)

```json
{
  "clientId": "123456789",
  "firstName": null,
  "lastName": null,
  "businessName": null,
  "AcctStatus": "A",
  "customerSites": [
    {
      "externalSiteId": "5113305555",
      "isPrimary": true,
      "firstName": "John",
      "lastName": "Doe",
      "address1": "123 Main St.",
      "city": "Detroit",
      "state": "MI",
      "postalCode": "48067",
      "meters": [
        {
          "accountNumber": "85000000",
          "meterId": "123456789",
          "meterType": "Electric",
          "unitOfMeasure": "kWh",
          "isPrimary": true,
          "isAMI": true,
          "isAMR": true,
          "rateCode": "ABCRATE1",
          "billingCycleId": 1
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

### Customer fields

| Field | Data type | Required | Notes |
|-------|-----------|----------|-------|
| `clientId` | Alphanumeric | **Yes** | Unique customer identifier. Use a permanent profile ID (BPID, BPN, or Profile ID) so the record persists across moves. |
| `firstName` | String | Optional | Customer's first name. |
| `lastName` | String | Optional | Customer's last name. |
| `businessName` | String | Optional | If present, EnergyGrid marks the customer as a business account. |
| `AcctStatus` | String | Optional | Current account state. See [Appendix B](#account-status-codes). The API returns this field name in PascalCase. |
| `customerSites` | Array | **Yes** | Premises associated with the customer. |

### CustomerSite fields

| Field | Data type | Required | Notes |
|-------|-----------|----------|-------|
| `externalSiteId` | Alphanumeric | **Yes** | Premise or site number. Use the permanent value if available. With the account number, it identifies one premise in EnergyGrid. |
| `isPrimary` | Boolean | **Yes** | `true` if this is the customer's primary location. Always `true` if only one site exists. |
| `firstName` | String | Optional | First name on the billing account. |
| `lastName` | String | Optional | Last name on the billing account. |
| `address1` | String | **Yes** | Street address. |
| `city` | String | **Yes** | City. |
| `state` | String | **Yes** | Two-character state or province code. |
| `postalCode` | String | **Yes** | US: 5-digit zip code. Canada: 6-character postal code with space (for example, `V6M 2T5`). |
| `meters` | Array | **Yes** | Meters at this site. A site can have more than one meter of any type. |

### Meter fields

| Field | Data type | Required | Notes |
|-------|-----------|----------|-------|
| `accountNumber` | Alphanumeric | Conditional | Contract account number. **Required** if permanent client and premise IDs are used (where only the account number changes on move). Apply the same account number to all meters at a billing account. Account numbers must differ across premises. |
| `meterId` | Alphanumeric | **Yes** | Permanent unique meter identifier. Used for DataBridge Hub binding requests if applicable. |
| `meterType` | String | **Yes** | `"Electric"` or `"Gas"`. |
| `unitOfMeasure` | String | Optional | Electric: `kWh` or `Wh`. Gas: `ccf` or `cm`. |
| `isPrimary` | Boolean | **Yes** | `true` for the main meter when multiple meters exist at a site. If a site has an interruptible HVAC meter and a standard meter, the standard meter is marked primary. |
| `isAMI` | Boolean | **Yes** | `true` if this is an Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) smart meter. AMI meters have radios that form a mesh network and send data automatically. If `isAMI = true`, a DataBridge Hub can be added. |
| `isAMR` | Boolean | Optional | `true` if this is an Automated Meter Reading (AMR) meter, which a passing vehicle reads over RFID. |
| `PANID` | Alphanumeric | Optional | **Obsolete.** Personal Area Network (PAN) ID of the AMI meter. Previously used by DataBridge Hub for mesh binding. |
| `rateCode` | Alphanumeric | **Yes** | Meter rate code that determines which billing calculator to use. See [Step 6](#step-6-rate-information-required-for-billsense-ai). |
| `rateMultiplier` | Numeric | Optional | **Obsolete.** Rate multiplier for usage computation. |
| `billingCycleId` | Integer | **Yes** | Customer's billing cycle ID. References the billing cycle schedule. See [Step 5](#step-5-billing-cycle-schedule). |
| `dialCount` | Integer | Optional | **Obsolete.** Number of dials on a meter, previously used for AMR gas meters. |

:::tip Minimum fields for launch
The customer response must include at least: `clientId`, at least one `customerSite` with `externalSiteId` and `postalCode`, and at least one meter with `meterId`, `meterType`, `isAMI`, `rateCode`, and `billingCycleId`.
:::

## Step 4: Bulk data ingestion (required for BillSense AI)

The PowerBox API tells EnergyGrid who the customer is. To explain a bill, BillSense AI also needs how much energy the customer used and what they were charged.

:::caution
Without billing data and rate information, BillSense AI can't work. Projected bills won't match real bills, and customers call your support line to ask why.
:::

### 4.1 Usage data (MDM)

Usage data drives every chart in the app. It comes from your meter data management (MDM) system.

| Attribute | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| **Source** | Meter Data Management (MDM) system |
| **Electric granularity** | 15-minute or hourly |
| **Gas granularity** | Daily (standard) or hourly (if using AMR adapters) |
| **Latency** | Varies by utility, from a few hours to about 36 hours behind |

:::note AMI dependency
Without AMI meters and hourly data, there's little for the app to chart or analyze, and the platform loses most of its value.
:::

#### Ingestion methods

- **Full batch:** send data for every customer. EnergyGrid stores it and loads it when a customer registers.
- **Registered only:** send data only for customers who have registered.
- **API backfill:** EnergyGrid requests history through the API at registration, then regular SFTP or object-storage updates start the next day.

#### File format

**Format:** CSV via SFTP

**File naming convention:**

- Electric: `CompanyCode_DDMMYYYY_Electric.csv`
- Gas: `CompanyCode_DDMMYYYY_Gas.csv`

**CSV structure:**

```csv
AccountNumber,ExternalSiteID,MeterID,TimeStamp,TotalUnit
910020087577,5113018555,5532879,1/1/2017,22.556
910020087577,5113018555,5532879,1/2/2017,12.898
910020087577,5113018555,5532879,1/3/2017,0.256
910020087577,5113018555,5532879,1/4/2017,10.256
```

:::note
EnergyGrid loads data only for registered customers, matched by the identifiers from `/powerbox/customer`. You can still send data for every customer.
:::

### 4.2 Billing and financial data

To explain why a bill changed, for example because the rate went up, BillSense AI needs detailed billing data.

#### Meter Contract History (MCH)

The meter contract history (MCH) is the record of what the customer was billed. Include these fields:

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| Contract account | Billing account identifier |
| Billing start date | Start of the billing period |
| Billing end date | End of the billing period |
| Total consumption | Total energy used in the period |
| Usage value | Usage in billing units |
| Cost | Amount charged, in dollars |
| Tax amounts | Tax breakdown |
| Meter effective date | When the meter became active for this contract |

:::tip
Billing line items, with every charge broken out, work best. If you can't export them, the fields above are enough. You can usually drop about 25% of the columns in a typical billing export.
:::

#### Other data sets

| Data set | Description | Frequency |
|----------|-------------|-----------|
| **Invoice details** | Line items (taxes, fees, riders). BillSense AI uses them to attribute each charge. | Daily |
| **Payment plans** | Customers on payment arrangements or budget billing | Daily |
| **Account termination** | Closed accounts, so EnergyGrid can delete their data | Daily, or as needed |

:::note Solar billing
Solar billing varies a lot between utilities. EnergyGrid supports net metering today and handles other solar structures case by case.
:::

## Step 5: Billing cycle schedule

Billing cycles, also called the meter reading schedule or meter reading units (MRU), define the periods customers are billed for. The `billingCycleId` on each meter references this schedule.

Utilities stagger billing cycles to spread the processing load, often around 100,000 customers per cycle per day. A utility can have as few as 20 cycles or several thousand MRUs.

EnergyGrid needs the complete schedule to calculate the costs of each billing period.

### Example: cycle 1 schedule for 2025

| Cycle ID | Start date | End date |
|----------|-----------|----------|
| 1 | 2024-12-03 | 2025-01-02 |
| 1 | 2025-01-03 | 2025-01-30 |
| 1 | 2025-01-31 | 2025-03-03 |
| 1 | 2025-03-04 | 2025-04-01 |
| 1 | 2025-04-02 | 2025-05-01 |
| 1 | 2025-05-02 | 2025-06-02 |
| 1 | 2025-06-03 | 2025-07-02 |
| 1 | 2025-07-03 | 2025-08-01 |
| 1 | 2025-08-02 | 2025-09-02 |
| 1 | 2025-09-03 | 2025-10-01 |
| 1 | 2025-10-02 | 2025-10-30 |
| 1 | 2025-10-31 | 2025-12-02 |

:::note
Cycle IDs can be alphanumeric, depending on your system.
:::

## Step 6: Rate information (required for BillSense AI)

:::warning Required
Without rate information, BillSense AI can't calculate a bill. Projections won't match real bills, and customers call your support line to ask why.
:::

The `rateCode` on each meter tells EnergyGrid which billing calculator to use. Send every rate code you offer for **residential** customers.

### Meter rate codes

| Rate code | Description |
|-----------|----------------------|
| EFR_D1_8 | Residential Dynamic Peak Pricing, Exp. D1_8 |
| EFR_D1-A | Residential Time-of-Day Pilot I |
| EFR_D1-B | Residential Time-of-Day Pilot II |
| EFR_D1.11 | Residential Service Rate, Standard Time-of-Use D1.11 |
| EFR_D1.13 | Residential Service Rate, Overnight Savers |

### Supported rate types

EnergyGrid supports three ways to calculate rates. Fixed costs (service and facility fees, taxes, and non-taxable program charges) apply on top of any of them.

#### Time of use (TOU)

TOU rates need:

- A schedule of observed holidays (generally treated as off-peak)
- Peak intervals with start and end hours for each day type

**Example: summer TOU schedule**

| Name | Amount ($/kWh) | Start hour | End hour | Rate start date | Rate end date |
|------|---------------|------------|----------|----------------|--------------|
| Off-peak M-F | 0.0479 | 0 | 7 | 2025-06-01 | 2025-09-30 |
| Mid-Peak M-F | 0.0922 | 7 | 15 | 2025-06-01 | 2025-09-30 |
| On-peak M-F | 0.1660 | 15 | 19 | 2025-06-01 | 2025-09-30 |
| Off-Peak M-F | 0.0479 | 23 | 24 | 2025-06-01 | 2025-09-30 |
| Off-Peak Wknd/Holiday | 0.0479 | 0 | 24 | 2025-06-01 | 2025-09-30 |

EnergyGrid splits each day into intervals on a 24-hour clock. Weekends and holidays count as off-peak. The start and end dates define the summer period. Winter periods follow the same structure with different amounts, typically running from October 1 to May 31, then cycling back to summer rates.

Concurrent rates (delivery, energy waste reduction, distribution) can be rolled into the peak windows or evaluated separately.

#### Tiered

Tiered rates use a prorate factor for the daily Tier 1 allowance. For example, with a factor of 22.1918 kWh a day, a 30-day billing period has a Tier 1 limit of about 665.75 kWh. Usage above that limit is priced at Tier 2 for the rest of the period. Delivery, distribution, and other charges still apply.

#### Flat

One price per kWh for all usage.

## Step 7: Hardware binding (optional)

If your rollout includes the DataBridge Hub, the bind endpoint links the device to the customer's AMI meter over your wireless mesh radio.

**Endpoint:** `POST /powerbox/bind`

Binding uses a service account, not the customer's credentials. Each request carries a basic authentication header and, during the TLS 1.2 handshake, a client certificate for mutual TLS (mTLS) that EnergyGrid provides.

### Request payload

```json
{
  "hemProfileId": "a3f1c8d2-44bc-4e1a-b9f0-5c2e7d81a6b4",
  "macAddress": "70:B3:D5:4A:1C:9E",
  "installCode": "A1B2C3D4E5F6A7B8",
  "meterId": "123456789",
  "actionCode": 1
}
```

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| `hemProfileId` | EnergyGrid customer profile ID (GUID) |
| `macAddress` | MAC address on the DataBridge Hub label |
| `installCode` | Install code on the same label |
| `meterId` | Meter to bind, from customer sync |
| `actionCode` | `1` to bind, `0` to release the meter |

### Response

`200` with no body means the request was accepted. Pairing finishes afterward, usually within 15 minutes and at most 48 hours.

Binding isn't idempotent. A second bind for the same meter returns `400`:

```json
{
  "errorCode": "METER_ALREADY_BOUND",
  "message": "Meter 123456789 is already bound. Send actionCode 0 to release it first."
}
```

For the other error codes, see [Appendix A](#error-codes).

## Step 8: Data transport options

EnergyGrid can exchange bulk data in any of these ways:

| Method | Notes |
|--------|-------|
| **SFTP** | Standard method for MDM data |
| **FTP** | Legacy option |
| **Object-storage replication** | Bucket-to-bucket sync between your object store and EnergyGrid's |
| **API** | On-demand backfill or real-time feeds |
| **File exchange** | A generic file drop |

At the integration kickoff, agree on the method and on who hosts it, you or EnergyGrid.

## Appendix A: Error codes {#error-codes}

| HTTP status | Error code | Description |
|-------------|-----------|-------------|
| 401 | 1 | Invalid credentials. The customer does not have a utility account. |
| 401 | 2 | Invalid credentials. Two authentication attempts remaining. |
| 401 | 3 | Invalid credentials. One authentication attempt remaining. |
| 401 | 4 | Account is locked. The customer must contact the utility to remove the lock. |
| 401 | 86 | Account is closed, finaled, or no longer accessible. EnergyGrid might still have a record for it. |
| 503 | None | PowerBox API outage or maintenance. The response has no body. |

:::note
Error codes 2 to 4 apply only to existing utility customers.
:::

## Appendix B: Account status codes {#account-status-codes}

| Status code | Name | Description |
|-------------|------|-------------|
| A | Active | Active account |
| C | Charge off | Account charged off |
| D | Active service disconnect | Active account with service disconnected |
| F | Final | Final account billing complete |
| L | Closed | Closed account with unpaid final bill |
| N | New | Active new account |
| P | Pending | Pending account with a future open date |
| S | Sold | Sold receivables account |
| U | Final account funds due | Final account with unclaimed funds |
| X | Final account still billed | Final account still receiving charges |
| Z | Cancel | Cancelled account |

---

URL: https://l-g99921.github.io/tw-portfolio/docs/databridge/databridge-installation-guide-atlas-insight

# DataBridge installation guide

This guide shows you how to install the DataBridge Hub at home and connect it to your smart meter. It takes about 15 minutes, plus the time your utility takes to approve the connection.

:::info Which guide is this?
Each utility that offers the DataBridge Hub publishes its own version of this guide. This is the version for **Atlas Insight** customers. For Pacific Grid, see the [DataBridge Hub setup guide](./databridge-hub-setup-guide-pacific-grid).
:::

## Before you begin

Have these ready:

- **EnergyGrid app:** download it from the App Store or Google Play.
- **EnergyGrid account:** an active account linked to your service address.
- **A phone with Bluetooth:** iPhone or Android.
- **A 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi network:** the DataBridge Hub doesn't work with 5 GHz networks.
- **The power adapter:** check that the micro-USB adapter is in the box.

## Physical setup

1. **Power the device**

    Plug the adapter into the micro-USB port on the back of the DataBridge Hub, then into a wall outlet.

2. **Connect to the network**

    To use a cable, plug an Ethernet cable into the square port on the DataBridge Hub and connect the other end to your router. A cable gives the most stable connection, but it's optional. To use Wi-Fi instead, skip this step. The app connects the hub to Wi-Fi [later](#wi-fi-connection).

    :::tip
    If you change your mind, the app offers an Ethernet option during the Wi-Fi step.
    :::

3. **Check the status light**

    Wait for the light on the front of the device to turn solid green before you continue.

## Mobile app setup

With the hub powered on, use the EnergyGrid app to connect it to your account.

### Start setup

1. **Begin the installation**

    Open the EnergyGrid app and tap **Begin DataBridge Setup**. You can also find it under **My Devices**.

2. **Check the requirements**

    The first screen lists what you need before you continue. The app then guides you through each step.

### Pairing

1. **Scan for the device**

    Tap **Start Scanning**.

2. **Pair over Bluetooth**

    Hold the phone against the DataBridge Hub. The light turns blue when pairing starts.

### Wi-Fi connection

1. **Select the network**

    Choose your home Wi-Fi network from the list. If it appears twice, choose the 2.4 GHz one.

2. **Enter the password**

    Type the Wi-Fi password and tap **Continue**.

### Meter binding

:::caution Stay in range
Keep the DataBridge Hub within 30 feet (about 9 meters) of your smart meter until binding finishes. The hub has to stay reachable on the meter's home area network.
:::

1. **Request the bind**

    Tap **Request Bind**. Your utility receives the request and adds the hub to the meter's home area network (HAN), so it can read your usage directly from the meter.

2. **Wait for the connection**

    Binding usually finishes within 15 minutes. With a weak signal, it can take up to 48 hours. Keep the hub plugged in and close to the meter until then.

### Finish setup

1. **Confirm successful connection**

    When setup is complete, the **Successfully Connected** screen appears, and your usage starts showing in the app.

## Troubleshooting

| Problem | Cause | What to do |
|-------|-------|----------|
| The light doesn't turn solid green | The adapter isn't fully plugged in | Push the adapter firmly into the micro-USB port and the outlet, or try another outlet. If the light stays off or flashes red, contact EnergyGrid support. |
| The Bluetooth scan doesn't find the hub | Bluetooth is off, or the phone is too far away | Turn on Bluetooth and hold the phone a few inches from the hub. Restart the app and scan again. If the hub still doesn't appear, unplug it for 10 seconds and plug it back in. |
| Binding hasn't finished | The hub is too far from the meter, or the utility network is slow | Move the hub within 30 feet (about 9 meters) of the meter. Binding can take up to 48 hours. If it hasn't finished after 48 hours, tap **Request Bind** again, and contact EnergyGrid support if it still doesn't work. |

---

URL: https://l-g99921.github.io/tw-portfolio/docs/smartlink/smartlink-installation-guide

# SmartLink Plug installation guide

This guide shows you how to install the SmartLink Plug and link it to your smart meter with the EnergyGrid app. Setup takes about 10 minutes. After that, your utility can take 24 to 48 hours to finish linking the plug to the meter. To learn what the SmartLink Plug does, see [Products](/docs/#products).

## Before you begin

Gather these items before starting the installation.

### Requirements

- SmartLink Plug
- EnergyGrid app installed on iOS or Android
- EnergyGrid account credentials (administrator access required)
- Home Wi-Fi network name and password
- Wi-Fi enabled on the mobile device
- Standard wall outlet within 30 feet (9 meters) of the utility smart meter

:::tip
Use the 2.4 GHz network if your router broadcasts separate 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz networks.
:::

### Placement guidelines

Choose a location that meets all of the following criteria:

- On the same side of the house as the smart meter
- With minimal walls or large appliances between the SmartLink Plug and the meter
- Within 30 feet (9 meters) of the smart meter

:::warning
Do not place the SmartLink Plug directly behind the meter, near metal racks, near electrical panels, or behind large appliances. These locations interfere with the wireless signal.
:::

## Mobile app setup

Power on the SmartLink Plug first. Then use the EnergyGrid app to connect the device to your account.

### Sign in

1. **Open the app**

    Launch the EnergyGrid app on your mobile device.

2. **Enter your credentials**

    Type your EnergyGrid account username and password. Administrator access is required.

### Start setup

1. **Open the Toolkit**

    Tap the **Toolkit** icon in the navigation bar at the bottom of the screen.

2. **Begin setup**

    Locate the SmartLink Plug card and tap **Set Up**. Tap **Begin Setup** on the welcome screen.

### QR code scanning

1. **Grant camera access**

    Tap **Allow** when prompted to grant camera access.

2. **Scan the code**

    Locate the QR code on the back of the SmartLink Plug. Hold the QR code in front of the phone camera until it comes into focus. A blue checkmark appears when the scan succeeds. The app uses the QR code to identify the device and prepare the Wi-Fi connection.

### Physical setup

1. **Plug in the device**

    Insert the SmartLink Plug into a standard wall outlet within 30 feet (9 meters) of the smart meter.

2. **Check the LED**

    Wait for the LED indicator to pulse blue. This indicates the SmartLink Plug is ready to connect.

3. **Continue in the app**

    Tap **Continue** in the app.

:::note
If the LED does not pulse blue, tap **Need Help?** in the top-right corner of the screen for troubleshooting options.
:::

### Wi-Fi connection

1. **Connect to the SmartLink network**

    The SmartLink Plug creates a temporary Wi-Fi network to communicate with your phone. A prompt appears asking you to join this network (displayed as "EBX_000-00000X" or similar). Tap **Join**.

2. **Select your home network**

    Choose your home Wi-Fi network from the list. Select the 2.4 GHz network.

3. **Enter the password**

    Type the Wi-Fi password and tap **Continue**.

### Meter binding

1. **Submit the request**

    The app automatically submits a bind request to the utility after the Wi-Fi connection is established. This request authorizes the SmartLink Plug to communicate with the smart meter.

2. **Wait for processing**

    The utility typically accepts the bind request within 5 minutes. After the utility accepts the bind request, live energy data can take 24–48 hours to appear in the app.

:::caution
Keep the SmartLink Plug within 30 feet of the smart meter and powered on throughout the binding period.
:::

The **Bind Request Complete** screen confirms a successful request.

## Verify installation

Check these indicators after the utility processes the bind request, which typically takes 24–48 hours.

### Success indicators

- The SmartLink Plug LED displays a steady state and is not flashing an error pattern
- Real-time energy usage data appears in the EnergyGrid app
- The SmartLink Plug appears as connected in the Toolkit section of the app

## Troubleshooting

### No connection after 5 minutes

1. **Check power**

    Verify the SmartLink Plug is inserted into the outlet and the LED is on.

2. **Improve placement**

    Move the SmartLink Plug to an outlet closer to the smart meter with fewer walls between them.

3. **Power cycle**

    Unplug the device, wait 10 seconds, then plug it back in.

4. **Verify Wi-Fi**

    Confirm the home Wi-Fi network is functioning properly.

### Communication error during setup

1. **Verify Wi-Fi**

    Confirm that Wi-Fi is enabled on your mobile device and that you are connected to the correct network.

2. **Check signal strength**

    Move closer to the SmartLink Plug. Ensure no large appliances or metal objects are between the phone and the device.

3. **Retry**

    Tap **Try Again** to retry the connection.

### LED not pulsing blue

1. **Power cycle**

    Unplug the device and wait 10 seconds.

2. **Wait for activation**

    Plug the device back in and wait up to 60 seconds for the LED to activate.

3. **Contact support**

    Contact your utility support team if the LED still does not pulse blue.

## Support

Contact your utility support team for assistance.

- **In-app chat:** Open the EnergyGrid app and go to **Menu > Support Center**.
- **Phone and email:** Contact your utility provider for current support channels and hours.

# BillSense AI overview

BillSense AI explains a customer's energy bill. It combines the bill with the customer's meter readings and home profile, shows where the energy went, explains why the bill changed, and suggests ways to save.

These pages are for the utility support agents who walk customers through it.

## What it does

- Compares each bill with the previous month and the same month last year.
- Splits usage into categories, such as heating, cooling, and appliances.
- Suggests savings based on the customer's usage and home.
- Compares the home with similar homes nearby.
- Suggests a rate plan that might cost less.
- Shows past bills and yearly totals.

## What it can't do

- **Show the full bill amount.** Totals leave out taxes, fees, and voluntary program charges. The bill statement is the official amount.
- **Match the meter exactly.** kWh values are estimates and can differ slightly from the bill.
- **Make good suggestions from a wrong profile.** If the appliances in **My Home** are wrong, the recommendations will be too.
- **Change a fixed-term plan.** Customers on a fixed-term rate agreement can't switch plans until it ends.

## Where to go next

- [Before you begin](./before-you-begin): what you need, how to open BillSense AI, and how to escalate.
- [User guide](./): each section of BillSense AI, and how to walk a customer through a billing question.
- [Troubleshooting](./troubleshooting): symptoms and fixes.
- [Glossary](./glossary): energy and billing terms used in the tool.

---

URL: https://l-g99921.github.io/tw-portfolio/docs/billsense-ai/troubleshooting

# Troubleshooting

For utility support agents answering questions about BillSense AI. Find the customer's symptom below. If it isn't listed, or the steps don't solve it, follow the [escalation path](./before-you-begin#if-you-cannot-resolve-the-issue).

## BillSense AI doesn't load

1. **Check the sign-in**

    Confirm the customer is signed in to the Utility Portal.

2. **Allow pop-ups and JavaScript**

    Confirm the browser allows pop-ups and JavaScript for the portal. If the customer doesn't know how, point them to their browser's help.

3. **Clear the cache**

    Ask the customer to clear the browser's cache and cookies, then reload the page.

4. **Try another browser**

    Test with a different web browser.

## The numbers don't match the paper bill

1. **Explain what's left out**

    BillSense AI totals don't include taxes, fees, or voluntary program charges.

2. **Explain the kWh difference**

    The kWh values in BillSense AI are estimates and can differ slightly from the metered values on the bill.

3. **Point to the bill**

    The bill statement is the official breakdown. Ask the customer to check it for the exact amounts.

## Recommendations don't fit the customer's home

1. **Open My Home**

    Go to **My Home** in BillSense AI.

2. **Check the appliances**

    Confirm that heating, cooling, and cooking match what the customer has.

3. **Check electric vehicle details**

    If the customer has an electric vehicle (EV), confirm it's listed with the right charger type.

4. **Wait for the update**

    Recommendations refresh within 24 hours of a profile change.

## The customer mentions a light or a connection problem

BillSense AI is a web tool, with no device or lights. The customer is probably describing their DataBridge Hub or SmartLink Plug. Use the [DataBridge Hub guide](/docs/databridge/databridge-installation-guide-atlas-insight#troubleshooting) or the [SmartLink Plug guide](/docs/smartlink/smartlink-installation-guide#troubleshooting).

# Data dictionary

This reference lists the data sets behind EnergyGrid integrations: what each one depends on, which customers it covers, and where it's stored. Utilities integrate in one of three ways, depending on the data they can provide, so each integration type has its own table.

## How to read the tables

- **Depends on** lists the data sets that have to load first.
- **Customers** says whose data is stored: all of the utility's customers, only customers registered in the EnergyGrid app, or only customers with a DataBridge Hub or SmartLink Plug.
- **Where it lives** gives the database instance, then the database, schema, or table. "Read replica" means a read-only copy of the instance is available for queries.
- `public.*_usage` means every table in the `public` schema whose name ends in `_usage`.

## Integration type A

| Data set | Depends on | Customers | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|---|
| MDM usage data | Customer data | All | **MDM RDS:** `mdmusage`. **Object storage:** electric and gas MDM files. |
| MDM usage data (app copy) | Customer data | Registered | **Brainstem RDS** (read replica): `brainstem`, tables `public.*_usage`, hourly and coarser |
| Payment plans | Customer data, MCH billing data | All | **CorePlatform RDS:** `EGCore_UDX`, table `dbo.PaymentPlans`. **Object storage:** payment plan files. |
| Customer data | None | Registered | **CorePlatform RDS:** `EGCore_ATLS`. **CorePlatform Central RDS:** every database on the instance. **Brainstem RDS** (read replica): `brainstem`, tables listed in [Customer tables](#customer-tables). |
| BillSense AI data | Customer, MDM usage, billing, disaggregation, and data warehouse data | All | **MDM RDS:** `atls_bill_sense`. **Object storage:** BillSense AI files. Staging buckets and intermediate tables are in the BillSense AI integration runbook. |
| Meter contract history (MCH) billing data | Customer data | All | **Brainstem RDS** (read replica): `brainstem`, table `data.meter_contract_history`. **Object storage:** MCH files. |
| Disaggregation data | Customer data, MDM usage data | All | **Brainstem RDS** (read replica): `brainstem`, table `data.ntg_daily_disaggregation_partitioned` |
| Device minute usage | Customer data, a DataBridge Hub or SmartLink Plug | With a device | **Brainstem RDS** (read replica): `brainstem`, tables `public.*_usage`, per minute and coarser. **Object storage:** home minute usage, device minute usage, AMR gas hourly usage, and heartbeats. |
| Powernet minute usage | Customer data, device minute usage | With a device | **Brainstem RDS** (read replica): `brainstem`, tables `public.*_usage`, per minute and coarser |
| Data warehouse | Usage, billing, and disaggregation data | Varies by data set | Combines several data sets, including advisor and recommendation data. The schema is in the data engineering runbook. |

**What each feature needs:**

- **EnergyGrid app:** MDM usage, customer data, device minute usage, Powernet minute usage, and the data warehouse.
- **Bill management:** MDM usage, customer data, MCH billing, payment plans, BillSense AI data, the data warehouse, and disaggregation data.

## Integration type B

| Data set | Depends on | Customers | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|---|
| MDM usage data | Customer data | Registered | **MDM RDS:** `grcn_mdm_prod`. **Brainstem RDS** (read replica): `brainstem`, tables `public.*_usage`, hourly and coarser. **Object storage:** MDM usage files. |
| Customer data | None | Registered | **CorePlatform RDS:** `EGCore_GRCN`. **CorePlatform Central RDS:** every database on the instance. **Brainstem RDS** (read replica): `brainstem`, tables listed in [Customer tables](#customer-tables). |
| Disaggregation data | Customer data, MDM usage data | Registered | **Brainstem RDS** (read replica): `brainstem`, table `data.ntg_daily_disaggregation_partitioned` |
| Device minute usage | Customer data, a device, data warehouse data | With a device | **Brainstem RDS** (read replica): `brainstem`, tables `public.*_usage`, per minute and coarser. **Object storage:** home minute usage, device minute usage, AMR gas hourly usage, and heartbeats. |
| Powernet minute usage | Customer data, device minute usage | With a device | **Brainstem RDS** (read replica): `brainstem`, tables `public.*_usage`, per minute and coarser. **Object storage:** Powernet files. |
| Data warehouse | Usage, billing, and disaggregation data | Varies by data set | Combines several data sets, including advisor and recommendation data. The schema is in the data engineering runbook. |

**What each feature needs:**

- **EnergyGrid app:** MDM usage, customer data, device minute usage, Powernet minute usage, the data warehouse, and disaggregation data.

## Integration type C

| Data set | Depends on | Customers | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|---|
| MDM usage data | Customer data | All | **Object storage:** MDM files |
| MDM usage data (app copy) | Customer data | Registered | **Brainstem RDS** (read replica): `brainstem_spec`, tables `public.*_usage`, hourly and coarser |
| Customer data | None | Registered | **CorePlatform RDS:** `EGCore_SPEC`. **CorePlatform Central RDS:** every database on the instance. **Brainstem RDS** (read replica): `brainstem_spec`, tables listed in [Customer tables](#customer-tables). |
| Disaggregation data | Customer data, MDM usage data | All | **Brainstem RDS** (read replica): `brainstem_spec`, table `data.ntg_daily_disaggregation_partitioned` |
| Advisor data | Customer data, MDM usage data, and more for some advisor cards | Registered | **Data warehouse RDS** (read replica): `datawarehouse_spec`, tables `public.homecharacteristics` and `public.metrictypes`. Advisor settings are in the `coaching` schema of the same database. |

**What each feature needs:**

- **External API:** MDM usage, customer data, disaggregation data, and advisor data.

## Customer tables

In every integration type, customer data in Brainstem is spread across these tables:

| Table | Holds |
|---|---|
| `public.people` | Customers |
| `public.sites` | Service addresses (premises) |
| `public.person_site_associations` | Which customers belong to which premises |
| `public.things` | Meters and devices |
| `public.thing_properties` | Settings and attributes of each meter or device |
| `public.source_target_associations` | Links between meters and devices, such as a hub bound to a meter |
