# About PIX

PIX is Brazil's instant-payments system, run by the [Banco Central do Brasil](https://www.bcb.gov.br/en/financialstability/pix_en) (BCB). It moves money between accounts at hundreds of banks and fintechs in a few seconds, at any hour, on any day, including weekends and holidays.

This page explains how PIX works and why its API looks the way it does. It's written for people who design, document, or integrate payment APIs. It doesn't teach a specific API. For that, follow [Send your first PIX payment](./tutorial-first-payment).

## Why PIX exists

Before November 2020, moving money between Brazilian banks was slow. TED transfers settled on the same day, but only during banking hours. DOC transfers settled the next business day. Anything outside those windows waited.

PIX replaced that with one system that:

- Settles each payment individually, in seconds.
- Runs 24 hours a day, every day of the year.
- Is free for individuals. Businesses pay their own bank's fees, which are usually lower than card fees.
- Uses identifiers people already know, like a phone number, an email address, or a tax ID, instead of branch and account numbers.

It launched in November 2020 and reached [over a billion transactions a month](https://www.bcb.gov.br/en/financialstability/pix_en) within its first year. Today it's one of the largest instant-payment systems in the world, alongside India's UPI.

## Who's involved

Every PIX payment has two sides:

- The **payer**, who sends the money.
- The **payee**, the merchant or person who receives it.

Each side has an account at an institution licensed by the BCB, called a **payment service provider (PSP)**. Only PSPs connect to the central infrastructure. Everyone else, including merchants and most fintechs, integrates through a PSP's API.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Payer App
    participant Payer PSP
    participant SPI as PIX infrastructure (SPI)
    participant Payee PSP
    participant Payee App

    Payer App->>Payer PSP: Pay this PIX key
    Payer PSP->>SPI: Settlement request
    SPI->>Payee PSP: Credit notification
    Payee PSP->>Payee App: Webhook with e2eId
    Payer PSP-->>Payer App: Confirmation
    Note over SPI: The whole flow targets under 10 seconds
```

## What you integrate with

When a developer says they're "integrating PIX," they almost always mean a PSP's API, not the central infrastructure. The infrastructure is a [message network run by the BCB](https://www.bcb.gov.br/estabilidadefinanceira/pix) that only licensed institutions can join. PSPs expose an API on top of it for their business customers.

The BCB publishes a [standard for that PSP API](https://bacen.github.io/pix-api/). Its main resources:

| Resource | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `cob` | An immediate charge: a payment request the merchant creates and the customer pays. |
| `cobv` | A charge with a due date, and optional fines, interest, and discounts. |
| `pix` | A received payment, looked up by its `e2eId`. |
| `webhook` | A URL the PSP calls when a payment to a given key settles. |
| `lote` | A batch of due-date charges, for merchants with high volume. |

The [Instant Payments API sample](/docs/api/pix-api/instant-payments-api-pix-sample) on this site covers part of that standard: enough to create a charge, receive the payment, and reconcile it.

## PIX keys

A **PIX key** (`chave`) is an alias that points to a bank account. There are five types. The type decides who can register the key and how apps should show it:

| Type | Format | Who can register it | How apps show it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **CPF** | 11 digits | The person who owns the CPF | Partly masked, for example `***.456.789-**` |
| **CNPJ** | 14 digits | The company that owns the CNPJ | In full |
| **Email** | An email address | Anyone, after confirming the address | In lowercase |
| **Phone** | E.164, starting with `+55` | Anyone, after confirming by SMS | In international format |
| **Random key (EVP)** | A UUID generated by the PSP | Anyone | As a value to copy, rarely in full |

When a payer enters a key, their PSP looks it up in **DICT**, the key directory run by the BCB, to find which PSP holds the account and where to send the payment.

An account can have up to 5 keys if it belongs to a person, and up to 20 if it belongs to a company. A key can point to only one account.

### Why random keys exist

The random key, *chave aleatória*, is there for privacy. People who don't want to share their phone, email, or tax ID with whoever pays them use a random key instead. It's harder to read out over the phone and impossible to memorize, so apps share it as text to copy or as a QR code.

## End-to-end ID

Every settled payment gets an **end-to-end ID** (`e2eId`), and its format is fixed:

```
E + ISPB (8) + yyyyMMddHHmm + suffix (11)
```

| Part | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `E` | Fixed prefix |
| `ISPB` | The 8-digit code that identifies the payer's institution in the Brazilian payment system |
| `yyyyMMddHHmm` | Creation time in UTC, to the minute |
| `suffix` | 11 alphanumeric characters, unique within that minute |

The `e2eId` is the identifier to reconcile on. Webhooks, refund requests, and audit trails all reference it. If you store only one field about a PIX payment, store the `e2eId`.

## Charges and the `txid`

A `cob` is a payment request. The merchant creates it, and the central infrastructure doesn't know about it until someone pays. Each charge has a `txid`: an ID the merchant chooses, 26 to 35 letters and digits long, unique at that PSP for at least 365 days.

How they relate:

- One `txid` has at most one charge, and a charge has at most one settled `e2eId`.
- An `e2eId` has at most one `txid`. A PIX sent without a charge has none.

Merchants use the `txid` to connect a charge to their own order. The payment system uses the `e2eId` to identify the payment.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Order[Order 4821] -->|create| Txid[txid: INV4821a1b2...]
    Txid --> Cob[Charge: ATIVA]
    Cob -->|customer pays| Settle((Settlement))
    Settle --> E2eId[e2eId: E12345678...]
    Cob -->|status changes| Done[Charge: CONCLUIDA]
    E2eId -.->|webhook| Merchant[Merchant backend]
    Order -.->|match by txid| Merchant
```

## What "instant" means

The 10-second target covers the whole flow, from the moment the payer's PSP sends the payment to the moment the payee's PSP confirms the credit. Most of that time goes to processing inside each PSP.

This has consequences for integrators:

- **Payments can't be undone.** A settled PIX can't be reversed. A refund (*devolução*) is a new transaction that references the original. The BCB's special return mechanism (MED) covers fraud cases, through the PSPs.
- **Rely on webhooks, not polling.** Polling `GET /cob/{txid}` shows the status change from `ATIVA` to `CONCLUIDA`, but the webhook arrives sooner and carries the payment details.
- **Expect duplicates.** The central infrastructure settles each `e2eId` once, but a PSP can deliver the same webhook more than once. If you credit a customer twice, the only fix is a refund, which is another PIX. [Handle PIX webhooks](./how-to-handle-webhooks) shows how to avoid that.

## Why the API looks the way it does

Some conventions in the PIX standard surprise developers used to card APIs:

- **The merchant chooses the `txid`.** The client creates the charge with `PUT /cob/{txid}` at a URL it picked. A retry after a timeout hits the same URL instead of creating a second charge. A retry with the same body succeeds, and a different body returns `409`. A point-of-sale system can also create the ID before it has a connection.
- **`PUT` creates, `PATCH` changes.** That follows from the point above: the client knows the resource's URL in advance.
- **Amounts are strings.** For example, `"valor": { "original": "150.00" }`. JSON numbers are often parsed as floating point, which can't represent every decimal exactly. A string keeps the amount exact.
- **Field names are in Portuguese:** `cob`, `chave`, `devedor`, `valor`, `solicitacaoPagador`. PIX is national infrastructure, and the standard was written for Brazilian developers first.

Each of these choices prevents a kind of bug that shows up at high volume.

## Further reading

- [Banco Central do Brasil: PIX overview, in English](https://www.bcb.gov.br/en/financialstability/pix_en)
- [PIX PSP API standard, in Portuguese](https://bacen.github.io/pix-api/), the public OpenAPI specification the sample on this site is based on
- [BR Code manual](https://www.bcb.gov.br/estabilidadefinanceira/spb_pix), with the QR code format used in PIX charges
- [Send your first PIX payment](./tutorial-first-payment), a guided walkthrough in the sandbox
- [Handle PIX webhooks](./how-to-handle-webhooks), for a webhook listener ready for production
- [Instant Payments API reference](/docs/api/pix-api/instant-payments-api-pix-sample), the sample OpenAPI spec for this section

---

# Send your first PIX payment

In this tutorial you create a charge in the sandbox of the [Instant Payments API sample](/docs/api/pix-api/instant-payments-api-pix-sample), pay it with a simulated customer, receive the webhook, and reconcile the payment. By the end you'll have:

- An OAuth access token
- A charge, with its `txid`
- A webhook listener that receives payment notifications
- A settled payment with its `e2eId`, matched to the charge

You'll use `curl`, `jq`, and a short Node.js script for the webhook. Any HTTP client and language work if you prefer others.

If you want to understand PIX itself first, read [About PIX](./about-pix).

:::tip Try it in the browser
Every call except the webhook delivery also works on the [API reference pages](/docs/api/pix-api/instant-payments-api-pix-sample), in a sandbox the site simulates in your browser. Use any value as the token there.
:::

## Before you begin

- Node.js 20 or later, `curl`, and `jq`. To install `jq`, run `brew install jq` on macOS or `sudo apt install jq` on Debian and Ubuntu.
- An [ngrok](https://ngrok.com/) account. The free plan is enough.
- An empty folder:

    ```bash
    mkdir pix-tutorial && cd pix-tutorial
    ```

The sandbox doesn't move real money, so you can repeat any step.

## Step 1: Get an access token

1. **Request sandbox credentials**

    Email `pix-sandbox@instant-payments.example` with the subject `Sandbox access`. You get a `client_id` and a `client_secret` within one business hour.

    :::note
    This API is a portfolio sample, so this request flow is illustrative. The token request in the next steps is the one you'd make to a real PSP.
    :::

2. **Save them as environment variables**

    ```bash
    export PIX_CLIENT_ID=<your-client-id>
    export PIX_CLIENT_SECRET=<your-client-secret>
    export PIX_BASE_URL=https://sandbox.instant-payments.example/v2
    ```

3. **Request a token**

    PSPs use the OAuth 2.0 client credentials grant. Ask for the scopes this tutorial uses:

    ```bash
    PIX_TOKEN=$(curl -sS -X POST \
      "${PIX_BASE_URL%/v2}/oauth/token" \
      -u "$PIX_CLIENT_ID:$PIX_CLIENT_SECRET" \
      -d "grant_type=client_credentials&scope=cob.write cob.read pix.read webhook.write" \
      | jq -r .access_token)

    echo "Token: ${PIX_TOKEN:0:12}…"
    ```

    Expected output:

    ```text
    Token: eyJhbGciOiJ…
    ```

    The token lasts about one hour. If a later step returns `401`, request a new one.

## Step 2: Create a charge

A charge (`cob`) is a payment request that the customer pays. You choose its ID, the `txid`.

1. **Create a `txid`**

    ```bash
    export TXID=tutorial$(date +%Y%m%d%H%M%S)$(openssl rand -hex 4)
    echo "txid: $TXID (length ${#TXID})"
    ```

    A `txid` has 26 to 35 letters and digits. This one has 30.

2. **Create the charge**

    ```bash
    curl -sS -X PUT \
      "$PIX_BASE_URL/cob/$TXID" \
      -H "Authorization: Bearer $PIX_TOKEN" \
      -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      -d '{
        "calendario": { "expiracao": 3600 },
        "valor": { "original": "12.50" },
        "chave": "merchant@example.com",
        "solicitacaoPagador": "Tutorial run"
      }' | tee charge.json | jq .status
    ```

    Expected output:

    ```text
    "ATIVA"
    ```

    The full response is in `charge.json`. `ATIVA` means the charge is waiting for payment, for the next 3,600 seconds. `loc.location` is the payload a banking app reads from the QR code.

The key `merchant@example.com` is already registered to your sandbox client. In production, you use a PIX key registered to your own account.

## Step 3: Set up a webhook listener

When the payment settles, the PSP sends a webhook. Start a small server that prints what it receives, and make it reachable over HTTPS.

1. **Write the listener**

    Create `webhook.js`:

    ```javascript
    const http = require('http');

    http.createServer((req, res) => {
      let body = '';
      req.on('data', (chunk) => (body += chunk));
      req.on('end', () => {
        console.log(`\n${new Date().toISOString()}  ${req.method} ${req.url}`);
        try {
          console.log(JSON.stringify(JSON.parse(body), null, 2));
        } catch {
          console.log(body || '(empty body)');
        }
        res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' });
        res.end('{"received":true}');
      });
    }).listen(3000, () => console.log('Listening on http://localhost:3000'));
    ```

    Run it:

    ```bash
    node webhook.js
    ```

2. **Expose it with ngrok**

    In a second terminal:

    ```bash
    ngrok http 3000
    ```

    Expected output:

    ```text
    Forwarding  https://a1b2c3.ngrok.io -> http://localhost:3000
    ```

3. **Register the webhook**

    Replace the URL with the one ngrok printed:

    ```bash
    export NGROK_URL=https://a1b2c3.ngrok.io

    curl -sS -X PUT \
      "$PIX_BASE_URL/webhook/merchant@example.com" \
      -H "Authorization: Bearer $PIX_TOKEN" \
      -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      -d "{ \"webhookUrl\": \"$NGROK_URL/pix-callback\" }" | jq
    ```

    Expected output:

    ```json
    {
      "webhookUrl": "https://a1b2c3.ngrok.io/pix-callback",
      "chave": "merchant@example.com",
      "criacao": "2026-04-24T18:32:11Z"
    }
    ```

    A key has one webhook at most, so running this again replaces the URL. Following the PIX standard, the PSP adds `/pix` to the end of the URL when it calls you, so notifications arrive at `/pix-callback/pix`.

## Step 4: Pay the charge

In real life, the customer scans the QR code with their banking app. The sandbox has a helper endpoint that does it for you.

1. **Simulate the payment**

    ```bash
    curl -sS -X POST \
      "$PIX_BASE_URL/_sandbox/pay/$TXID" \
      -H "Authorization: Bearer $PIX_TOKEN" \
      -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      -d '{ "pagador": { "cpf": "12345678909", "nome": "João Tutorial" } }' \
      | jq -r .endToEndId
    ```

    Expected output:

    ```text
    E12345678202604241832A1B2C3D4E5F
    ```

    Save it for Step 5:

    ```bash
    export E2EID=E12345678202604241832A1B2C3D4E5F
    ```

2. **Check the webhook**

    In the terminal running `webhook.js`, the notification arrives within a few seconds. The body is a list, because one call can carry several payments:

    ```text
    2026-04-24T18:32:14.221Z  POST /pix-callback/pix
    {
      "pix": [
        {
          "endToEndId": "E12345678202604241832A1B2C3D4E5F",
          "txid": "tutorial20260424183205a1b2c3d4",
          "valor": "12.50",
          "horario": "2026-04-24T18:32:13Z"
        }
      ]
    }
    ```

:::warning Respond quickly
Return a `2xx` within 5 seconds. If you don't, the PSP retries with increasing delays for up to 24 hours, and you get the same payment again. [Handle PIX webhooks](./how-to-handle-webhooks) shows how to respond fast and process each payment once.
:::

## Step 5: Reconcile

The webhook tells you a payment arrived. The API confirms it.

1. **Read the charge again**

    ```bash
    curl -sS "$PIX_BASE_URL/cob/$TXID" \
      -H "Authorization: Bearer $PIX_TOKEN" \
      | jq '{ status, e2eId: .pix[0].endToEndId }'
    ```

    Expected output:

    ```json
    {
      "status": "CONCLUIDA",
      "e2eId": "E12345678202604241832A1B2C3D4E5F"
    }
    ```

    `CONCLUIDA` means the charge was paid. The charge now points to the payment, and the payment points back to the charge.

2. **Read the payment**

    ```bash
    curl -sS "$PIX_BASE_URL/pix/$E2EID" \
      -H "Authorization: Bearer $PIX_TOKEN" | jq
    ```

    Expected output:

    ```json
    {
      "endToEndId": "E12345678202604241832A1B2C3D4E5F",
      "txid": "tutorial20260424183205a1b2c3d4",
      "valor": "12.50",
      "horario": "2026-04-24T18:32:13Z",
      "pagador": {
        "cpf": "12345678909",
        "nome": "João Tutorial"
      }
    }
    ```

You created a charge, received the payment through a webhook, and confirmed it on both sides.

## What you built

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    OAuth[OAuth token] --> Charge["PUT /cob/{txid}<br/>(ATIVA)"]
    Charge --> Webhook["PUT /webhook/{chave}"]
    Webhook --> Pay["POST /_sandbox/pay<br/>(simulated)"]
    Pay --> Notify["Webhook<br/>(e2eId)"]
    Notify --> Reconcile["GET /cob/{txid}<br/>(CONCLUIDA)"]
```

A production integration makes the same calls. The part that has to scale is the webhook listener.

## Next steps

- [Handle PIX webhooks](./how-to-handle-webhooks): authentication, fast responses, processing each payment once, and recovering from an outage.
- [About PIX](./about-pix): keys, the `e2eId`, and why the API looks the way it does.
- [Instant Payments API reference](/docs/api/pix-api/instant-payments-api-pix-sample): every operation and field.

## Troubleshooting

| Problem | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `401` from `/oauth/token` | Wrong `client_id` or `client_secret` | Export the variables again and check for trailing spaces. |
| `400` from `PUT /cob/{txid}` about `valor.original` | The amount was sent as a number | Send it as a string: `"original": "12.50"`. |
| `400` from `PUT /cob/{txid}` about the `txid` | The `txid` is shorter than 26 or longer than 35 characters, or has symbols | Create a new one with the command in Step 2. |
| `409` from `PUT /cob/{txid}` | You reused a `txid` with a different body | Create a new `txid`, or send exactly the same body again. |
| No webhook arrives | The ngrok URL changed after you registered it | Register the webhook again with the current URL. |
| The same `e2eId` arrives twice | The PSP retried because your listener was slow | Store each `e2eId` and skip ones you've seen. See [Process each payment once](./how-to-handle-webhooks#process-each-payment-once). |

---

URL: https://l-g99921.github.io/tw-portfolio/docs/pix/how-to-handle-webhooks

# Handle PIX webhooks

This guide assumes you already create charges and receive webhooks in the sandbox. If you don't, start with the [tutorial](./tutorial-first-payment). A listener in production has to solve four problems:

1. Accept only requests that come from your PSP.
2. Respond within 5 seconds, even when your other systems are slow.
3. Process each payment once, even when the PSP delivers it twice.
4. Recover the payments it missed while it was down.

The examples use Node.js and Express. The same approach works in any stack.

## Know what arrives

Following the PIX standard, the PSP sends a `POST` to the URL you registered, with `/pix` added at the end. The body holds a list, because one call can carry several payments:

```json
{
  "pix": [
    {
      "endToEndId": "E12345678202604241832A1B2C3D4E5F",
      "txid": "tutorial20260424183205a1b2c3d4",
      "valor": "12.50",
      "horario": "2026-04-24T18:32:13Z",
      "infoPagador": "Order 4821"
    }
  ]
}
```

`txid` is empty for a PIX sent without a charge. The payer's name and tax ID aren't in the webhook. To get them, call `GET /pix/{e2eId}`.

## Authenticate the request

The PIX standard authenticates webhooks with **mutual TLS**: the PSP presents a client certificate, and your server accepts only certificates issued for your PSP. Set this up where TLS ends, usually in your load balancer or reverse proxy, and pass a header to the app saying the certificate checked out.

Many PSPs also sign each request with an HMAC of the body. If yours does, check the signature too.

1. **Keep the raw body**

    The HMAC covers the exact bytes the PSP sent. Parsing the JSON first changes spacing and key order, so the signature no longer matches.

    ```javascript
    const express = require('express');
    const crypto = require('crypto');

    const app = express();
    app.use('/pix-callback/pix', express.raw({ type: 'application/json' }));
    ```

2. **Compare signatures in constant time**

    ```javascript
    function verify(rawBody, headerSignature, secret) {
      const expected = crypto.createHmac('sha256', secret).update(rawBody).digest('hex');
      const a = Buffer.from(expected);
      const b = Buffer.from(headerSignature || '', 'utf8');
      return a.length === b.length && crypto.timingSafeEqual(a, b);
    }
    ```

    Use `crypto.timingSafeEqual`, not `===`. A plain comparison returns faster when the first bytes differ, and an attacker can measure that to guess the signature.

3. **Reject what fails**

    The header name depends on the PSP. Check your PSP's documentation.

    ```javascript
    function authenticate(req) {
      const mtlsOk = req.header('X-Client-Cert-Verified') === 'SUCCESS'; // set by your proxy
      const signature = req.header('X-Webhook-Signature');
      return mtlsOk && verify(req.body, signature, process.env.PIX_WEBHOOK_SECRET);
    }
    ```

:::warning Protect the secret
Anyone with the webhook secret can fake a payment confirmation. Keep it in a secret manager such as AWS Secrets Manager or HashiCorp Vault, never in a file in the repository, and rotate it when someone with access leaves the team.
:::

## Respond fast, process later

The PSP waits 5 seconds for a `2xx`. After that, it retries with increasing delays for up to 24 hours. A listener that writes to the database, updates balances, and notifies other systems before responding misses that limit under load.

Respond first and do the work afterward.

1. **Put each payment on a queue**

    ```javascript
    const { Queue } = require('bullmq');
    const pixQueue = new Queue('pix-webhooks', { connection: { host: process.env.REDIS_HOST } });

    app.post('/pix-callback/pix', async (req, res) => {
      if (!authenticate(req)) {
        return res.status(401).json({ error: 'unauthorized' });
      }

      const { pix = [] } = JSON.parse(req.body.toString('utf8'));
      for (const payment of pix) {
        await pixQueue.add('process', payment, {
          jobId: payment.endToEndId, // the queue ignores a second job with the same ID
          attempts: 5,
          backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 1000 },
        });
      }

      return res.status(200).json({ received: pix.length });
    });
    ```

    The handler authenticates, queues, and responds. Everything else happens in a worker.

2. **Process in a worker**

    ```javascript
    const { Worker } = require('bullmq');

    new Worker('pix-webhooks', (job) => recordPayment(job.data), {
      connection: { host: process.env.REDIS_HOST },
      concurrency: 50,
    });
    ```

    The worker can take as long as it needs, because the PSP already got its response.

The queue needs at-least-once delivery. BullMQ, Redis Streams, Amazon SQS, and Google Pub/Sub all provide it. The next section makes the occasional duplicate harmless.

## Process each payment once

Each `e2eId` settles only once, but you can still receive it more than once:

- Your first response took too long, and the PSP retried.
- Your response got lost on the network.
- The PSP failed over and resent messages in flight.
- A worker crashed halfway and the queue delivered the job again.

Use the `e2eId` as the idempotency key, and save it before anything with side effects happens.

1. **Let the database reject duplicates**

    ```sql
    CREATE TABLE pix_received (
      e2e_id        TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
      txid          TEXT,
      amount_cents  BIGINT NOT NULL,
      paid_at       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
      raw_payload   JSONB NOT NULL,
      processed_at  TIMESTAMPTZ
    );
    ```

    The primary key on `e2e_id` does the deduplication. If two workers race, the database decides, not your code.

2. **Insert first, then act on the result**

    ```javascript
    // "12.50" -> "1250". String math, no floating point. Returned as a string
    // so the driver passes it to the BIGINT column unchanged.
    function toCents(valor) {
      const [units, decimals = ''] = valor.split('.');
      return (BigInt(units) * 100n + BigInt(decimals.padEnd(2, '0').slice(0, 2))).toString();
    }

    async function recordPayment(payment) {
      const { rowCount } = await db.query(
        `INSERT INTO pix_received (e2e_id, txid, amount_cents, paid_at, raw_payload)
         VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, $5)
         ON CONFLICT (e2e_id) DO NOTHING`,
        [payment.endToEndId, payment.txid || null, toCents(payment.valor), payment.horario, payment],
      );

      if (rowCount === 0) return; // seen before

      await creditMerchant(payment);
      await notifyMerchantSystems(payment);
      await markProcessed(payment.endToEndId);
    }
    ```

    `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` needs one round trip. The first delivery inserts the row, and any later one changes nothing.

:::tip Keep the original body
Store the payload as received, in `raw_payload`. If someone disputes a payment months later, you'll want the exact webhook, not your processed version of it.
:::

## Recover after an outage

Listeners go down: a deploy, a database lock during a migration, a certificate that expires on a Sunday. The PSP retries for 24 hours, but your system shouldn't depend on that. Run a reconciler on a schedule that asks the API for received payments and feeds them through the same `recordPayment`.

1. **List payments received in a time window**

    The PIX standard has `GET /pix` with `inicio` and `fim` for the window, and paginates with `paginacao.paginaAtual`:

    ```javascript
    async function reconcile(startIso, endIso) {
      for (let page = 0, total = 1; page < total; page++) {
        const url = new URL(`${process.env.PIX_BASE_URL}/pix`);
        url.searchParams.set('inicio', startIso);
        url.searchParams.set('fim', endIso);
        url.searchParams.set('paginacao.paginaAtual', page);

        const res = await fetch(url, { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${await getToken()}` } });
        const body = await res.json();
        total = body.parametros.paginacao.quantidadeDePaginas;

        for (const payment of body.pix) {
          await recordPayment(payment); // duplicates are skipped by the primary key
        }
      }
    }
    ```

    Because `recordPayment` ignores payments it has already stored, replaying a whole window is safe.

2. **Run it on three schedules**

    | Every | Window | Catches |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | 5 minutes | Last 30 minutes | A webhook missed during normal operation |
    | Hour | Last 6 hours | Gaps from a short outage |
    | Day | Last 26 hours | Anything left before the PSP's 24-hour retries end |

    The three can overlap, because the database removes duplicates.

3. **Alert when the reconciler finds something new**

    If the reconciler stores a payment the webhook didn't, the live path failed. Record these on every run:

    ```text
    pix.reconciler.replayed{outcome=new}      = N   # payments the listener missed
    pix.reconciler.replayed{outcome=existing} = M   # already stored, which is normal
    pix.reconciler.lag_seconds                = K   # age of the oldest new payment
    ```

    Page someone when `outcome=new` goes above its usual daily level. A lag above 600 seconds means the listener is struggling.

## Production checklist

- [ ] mTLS required at the edge, and the HMAC checked if your PSP signs requests.
- [ ] Raw body kept until the signature check.
- [ ] Signatures compared with `timingSafeEqual`.
- [ ] Listener answers `2xx` within 5 seconds at p99.
- [ ] Each payment in the list queued with its `e2eId` as the job ID.
- [ ] `e2eId` is the primary key where payments are stored.
- [ ] Amounts converted from strings without floating point.
- [ ] Raw payload stored for audits.
- [ ] Reconciler running every 5 minutes, every hour, and every day.
- [ ] Alert on `outcome=new` routed to whoever is on call.
- [ ] Webhook secret in a secret manager, rotated when people leave.

- [Instant Payments API reference](/docs/api/pix-api/instant-payments-api-pix-sample), with the webhook operations

URL: https://l-g99921.github.io/tw-portfolio/blog/documenting-pix-lessons

From 2022 to 2024, through Zup Innovation, I owned the official documentation for Itaú's PIX APIs: 37+ endpoint references, integration guides, release notes, and migration guides, all in a docs-as-code pipeline on Bitbucket. Most of what I learned there I learned the usual way, by writing the wrong version first. These are the five lessons I'd pass on to anyone documenting a payments API.

<!--truncate-->

## Some context

PIX is Brazil's instant-payments system, run by the central bank (Banco Central do Brasil, or BCB). It launched in November 2020 and now handles [billions of transactions a month](https://www.bcb.gov.br/en/financialstability/pix_en). Most adults in Brazil use it.

Only licensed institutions, called PSPs, connect to the central infrastructure. Merchants, marketplaces, and apps integrate through a PSP's API. The BCB publishes a [standard for that API](https://bacen.github.io/pix-api/), and every PSP implements it. What differs from bank to bank is the documentation on top of the standard. That's where my work was.

## 1. The reference pages get the most traffic

Writing guides often treat the API reference as the easy part: generate it from the spec, link to it, and put the real effort into tutorials. In my experience with PIX, the reference page for `PUT /cob/{txid}` was the page people opened most. It came up in support tickets, incident reviews, audits, and every new engineer's first week.

That meant the reference had to be right and easy to scan:

- **Every status code documented**, including the ones that "shouldn't happen." A `409` on `PUT /cob/{txid}` happens. A `503` happens too.
- **Realistic examples.** A charge for `"150.00"` with a `solicitacaoPagador` in Portuguese, the way a real merchant would send it. People copy examples straight into their code.
- **Current behavior only.** If the page describes what the API did two versions ago, engineers stop trusting it and read the raw spec instead.

None of that is writing, really. It's a pipeline: the OpenAPI spec is the source, the reference pages are generated from it, and nobody edits the output by hand. Building and maintaining that pipeline took more of our time than any single page of prose.

## 2. Idempotency belongs on every page

The usual structure for API docs is overview, authentication, quickstart, endpoints, webhooks, and errors. For PIX, that put idempotency in the wrong place, buried in the errors page.

In PIX it touches everything. The merchant chooses the `txid`, and the PSP keeps it unique for at least 365 days. Each payment has an `e2eId` that settles exactly once, but the webhook carrying it can arrive more than once. So:

- Every page about a write operation explains what happens when you send it twice.
- Every webhook page says that your system, not the sender, is responsible for ignoring duplicates.
- The quickstart ends when you've stored the `e2eId` and a second delivery changes nothing, not when the first webhook arrives.
- The errors page separates a repeated `txid` with the same body, which is safe, from a repeated `txid` with a different body, which is a bug in the client.

We gave idempotency its own concept page and linked to it from every reference page. In the six months after that restructure, level 1 tickets on the PIX integration queue fell by about 45%, going by the tags in our ticketing system.

## 3. Keep the field names in Portuguese

The PIX standard is in Portuguese, and so are the field names (`cob`, `chave`, `devedor`, `valor`), the statuses (`ATIVA`, `CONCLUIDA`), and the error codes. English-speaking engineers on partner teams kept asking us to translate them.

We decided not to. The fields on the wire are in Portuguese. If the docs show English names, the integrator writes code against them, gets a `400`, finds the real names in the spec, and from then on doubts everything else the docs say.

What we did instead:

- Field names, example payloads, and error codes stay exactly as they are on the wire.
- The concepts get English names next to them on first mention: "charge (`cob`)," "PIX key (`chave`)."
- A glossary maps each Portuguese term to the English concept, with a one-line definition.

When a system has a canonical language, the docs should help people work with it, not hide it.

## 4. Most support questions are about webhooks

Our first webhook page was short: we send a `POST` to the URL you register. Meanwhile the request side, how to authenticate and create a charge, got most of the attention. That was backward. Integrators usually got the request side right on day one. The long support threads were about webhooks, and the same questions kept coming, roughly in this order:

1. "We're not receiving webhooks." Usually the endpoint wasn't reachable from the internet, or the certificate wasn't trusted.
2. "We received the same payment twice." The listener didn't return `2xx` in time, and the PSP retried.
3. "We credited a customer twice when the database was slow." They checked for the payment with a `SELECT` before the `INSERT`, instead of relying on a unique key.
4. "We lost payments during a deploy." The listener was down for longer than the retry window.
5. "The signature check fails." They verified the parsed JSON instead of the raw body.

Each of those was a documentation gap. We split the webhook content into three pages: the contract (authentication, payload, expected response), the production problems (authenticate, respond fast, deduplicate, recover), and reconciliation through the API. After that change, developer satisfaction with the docs went from 3.8 to 4.6 out of 5 in our quarterly developer experience survey (60+ responses), and integrators started linking to specific sections from their own runbooks.

The takeaway: spend documentation effort where the support tickets are, not evenly across endpoints.

## 5. The quickstart decides the integration

Many of the engineers reading our docs had never integrated an instant-payments system. For them, the quickstart was the first real test of whether the integration would go smoothly. What we learned about it:

- **It has to end with a settled payment and a webhook**, in the sandbox. A token or a created charge doesn't prove the integration works.
- **Every command has to work the first time.** One typo in step 4 and the reader stops trusting the rest.
- **It has to be one page.** Readers drop off between pages. One page they can scroll and copy from works better.
- **It should take 15 to 30 minutes.** Shorter means it skipped the hard parts, like duplicates and webhook handling, and the reader meets them in production instead.

We reviewed the quickstart more than any other page, and had engineers who had never seen the API run it before each release.

## What I'd do differently

We wrote the docs in roughly this order: reference, quickstart, concepts, errors, a webhook rewrite, reconciliation, idempotency as its own page, and the glossary.

Next time I'd write the concepts first, because every other page refers to them. Then the quickstart, because it forces each concept to be testable in half an hour. Then webhooks and reconciliation, where integrations succeed or fail. Reference last: once the structure around it is right, generating and checking it is mostly mechanical.

## What carries over to other APIs

- **Systems with a canonical language:** keep the wire names in the docs, and translate the concepts around them.
- **Webhook-heavy APIs:** give webhooks more than one page, and recommend a unique key in the database for deduplication.
- **APIs that teams pick during an evaluation:** treat the quickstart as the most important page on the site.

Some of the specifics are particular to PIX. Most APIs assign IDs on the server instead of letting the client choose them. Most international standards are published in English first. And a 24-hour retry window for webhooks is long compared with many other APIs.

# PowerBox API

The **PowerBox API** connects a utility's back-office systems to EnergyGrid. A utility needs two flows working before its customers can use EnergyGrid hardware or the app:

- **Customer sync:** send customer accounts, service addresses (premises), and meter configuration from the utility's customer information system (CIS) to EnergyGrid.
- **Hardware binding:** link a DataBridge Hub or SmartLink Plug to the customer's AMI meter over the utility's wireless mesh radio (home area network).

## Audience

Backend engineers at a utility who connect their CIS and AMI head-end systems to EnergyGrid. This isn't a public consumer API.

## Authentication

Every endpoint needs an OAuth 2.0 bearer token from the utility's identity provider. EnergyGrid doesn't issue tokens. They usually last one hour, and you refresh them through the utility IDP. Send the token in the `Authorization` header as `Bearer <token>`. For the full exchange, see [Configure authentication](/docs/integration-guide#step-2-configure-authentication-oauth) in the integration guide.

## Base URL

```
https://api.energygrid.example/v1
```

A staging environment is available for integration testing. Pick it in the **Servers** list on any operation page.

## Conventions

- **Content type.** `application/json` for requests and responses.
- **Identifiers.** `clientId`, `externalSiteId`, and `meterId` are strings owned by the utility CIS. EnergyGrid never generates them.
- **Account status.** `AcctStatus` uses the utility's own codes, such as `A` for active and `F` for final. EnergyGrid stores the value as received. For the full list, see [account status codes](/docs/integration-guide#account-status-codes).
- **Idempotency.** Customer sync is idempotent on `clientId`, so repeating it is safe. Binding isn't: a second bind for the same meter returns `400` with `METER_ALREADY_BOUND`.
- **Errors.** Errors use the HTTP status code. Login and bind errors also return an `errorCode` in the body. See [error codes](/docs/integration-guide#error-codes).

## Versioning

The version is in the path (`/v1`). Breaking changes ship as a new major version, and the old one stays available for at least 90 days. New optional fields and new values on extensible enums ship in the current version.

## Try it in the browser

Every operation page has a **Send API Request** panel. The hosts in this spec don't exist, so the site answers those requests in your browser with a simulated server built from this spec. Use any value as the bearer token.

## About this sample

EnergyGrid is a fictional platform, documented end to end on this site. The contracts and conventions reflect a realistic utility integration API. The hostnames don't resolve.

---

URL: https://l-g99921.github.io/tw-portfolio/usage-api-openapi.json

# EnergyGrid Usage API

The **EnergyGrid Usage API** is the read API behind the EnergyGrid app and partner web portals. It returns the consumption, budget, and insight data customers see, and every call is made as the signed-in customer, not as the utility.

The [PowerBox API](/docs/api/powerbox-api) moves data from the utility to EnergyGrid. The Usage API reads it back for one customer.

## Audience

Developers building partner mobile apps or white-label web portals that show energy use to customers.

## Authentication

Exchange a utility identity token for an EnergyGrid customer token with `POST /Customer/login`. Send the returned token as `Bearer <token>` on every other call. A token only reads data for the customer it belongs to. For the full handshake, see [Configure authentication](/docs/integration-guide#step-2-configure-authentication-oauth) in the integration guide.

## Base URL

```
https://api.energygrid.example/usage/v1
```

## Conventions

- **Content type.** `application/json`.
- **Granularity.** Usage endpoints take a `granularity` parameter. Read the valid values from `GET /MetaData/granularitytypes` instead of hard-coding them.
- **Currency and units.** Money is in the customer's billing currency. Energy is in the meter's `unitOfMeasure`, usually `kWh` for electricity.
- **Errors.** Errors follow [RFC 7807](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7807) problem details, with content type `application/problem+json`.

## Try it in the browser

Every operation page has a **Send API Request** panel. The hosts in this spec don't exist, so the site answers those requests in your browser with a simulated server built from this spec. Use any value as the bearer token.

## About this sample

The contracts reflect a realistic customer-facing usage API for a residential energy platform. EnergyGrid is fictional, and the hostnames don't resolve.

# Instant Payments API (PIX sample)

A sample API for creating and reconciling instant payments on PIX, Brazil's instant-payments system. The endpoints, payloads, and error codes follow the public PIX standard for payment service providers (PSPs) from Banco Central do Brasil. Customer identifiers, ISPBs, and webhook URLs are invented.

**This API is anonymized and synthetic.** I wrote it for this portfolio, based on the conventions I used on real PIX integrations: contract-first OpenAPI, one reference page per operation, and errors as RFC 7807 problem details.

## Try it in the browser

Every operation page has a **Send API Request** panel. The hosts in this spec don't exist, so the site answers those requests in your browser with a simulated server built from this spec. Use any value as the bearer token. Charges and webhooks keep state: create a charge with `PUT /cob/{txid}`, then read it with `GET` and change it with `PATCH`.
